R E P O R T
 
Roads are the very arteries of the nation, carrying the lifeblood of trade and commerce to all corners of the country,
 promoting and sustaining a robust national economy.  They also play an important role in national integration, which is
 particularly important in a country of the size of India.
 
2.         The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for development, formulation and implementation of
 policies relating to Road Transport and National Highways.  Its main function relate to road development and maintenance
 including Border Roads, Planning and co-ordination and Road Transport. The Ministry is administratively divided into two

D R A F T R E P O R T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/82ndreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:03:03]
 wings namely Transport Wing and Roads Wing.
 
3.         Transport Wing is concerned with the formulation of broad policies relating to Road Transport, Motor Vehicles Act,
 legislation relating to Road Transport Corporations, besides making arrangements for movement of motor vehicular traffic with
 the neighbouring countries.
 
            Roads Wing is mainly concerned with the matters relating to:-
(i)                  Advising Government on all general policy matters relating to Highways;
(ii)                Development & Maintenance of roads declared as National Highways;
(iii)               Roads other than National Highways in Union Territories;
(iv)              Administration of Central Road Fund (CRF) pertaining to State Roads other than rural roads;
(v)                Evaluation of standards for roads and bridges and formulation of specifications;
(vi)              Performance of road research;
(vii)             National Highways Authority of India and National Institute for Training of Highway Engineers.
 
4.         The following autonomous bodies function under the administrative control of the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways: -
 
(a)                National Highways Authority of India (NHAI); and
(b)                National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers (NITHE).
 
5.         Demand No.79 containing the details of budget allocation of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways for the
 financial year 2004-05, was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
 and Culture at its meeting held on the 13 th August 2004.  During the meeting, the Committee took oral evidence of the
 Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. 
 
PLAN PROVISIONS

 including National Highways.  This comprises of Rs.34,790 crore as Gross Budgetary Support and Rs.24,700 crore as Internal
 and Extra Budgetary Resources   (IEBR).

9.         While making presentation before the Committee during his evidence, the Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways brought out that the National Highway system in the country suffers from deficiencies of capacity constraint,

 inadequate pavement crust etc.  The resource requirement for removing deficiencies during Tenth Plan is around Rs.1,65,000
 crore.  However, the Tenth Plan allocation is only Rs.59,490 crore.  The Committee was further informed that the length of
 National Highway network other than NHDP is 51,290 kilometers and the pro-rata funds for maintenance and development for
 these highways are inadequate.  The Secretary also expressed the apprehension that National Highways Development Project
 (NHDP) may slide if funds assured for the project are not provided in future.
 
10.        According to the Tenth Five Year Plan, roads are the key to the development of an economy.  However, the allocations
 made for the road sector do not indicate their importance in the economic development of the country.  The Committee notes
 with concern that there is a huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during the Tenth Plan.  A good
 road network constitutes the basic infrastructure that propels the development process through connectivity and opening up the
 backward regions to trade and investment.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to achieve the objective of
 Tenth Plan in road sector, the budget allocation of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  The Committee notes that the Government has not been able to attract private investment as anticipated.  Therefore,
 the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan so as to
 reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
11.        India has a vast road network of 3.32 million kilometers of which the National Highways and the State Highways
 together account for 1,95,000 km.  As on 31
st March 2004, the length of National Highways network is only 65,569 km
 constituting about 2% of the total road network in the country and carrying about 40% of the total traffic across the length and
 breadth of the country.
 
12.        The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways is primarily responsible for the construction and maintenance of National
 Highways (NH). All roads, other than National Highway in States, fall within the jurisdiction of respective state governments. 
 The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on agency basis.  The National Highways Authority
 of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments (PWDs) and the Border Road Organisation (BRO) are the main agencies.
 Out of the total National Highway length of 65,569 km, about 14,279 km have been entrusted to National Highways Authority
 of India (NHAI) for improvement under National Highway Development Project (NHDP), Port Connectivity Schemes and
 other schemes.  The 7,457 km length of new National Highways is yet to be entrusted to agencies.  The balance lengths of
 about 39,129 km and 4,704 km of non-NHDP sections of National Highways are mainly entrusted to State PWDs and Border
 Road Organisation (BRO) respectively, as agencies of the Ministry. 
 
13.        Ministry of Road Transport & Highways has also decided to upgrade stretches of NH-34 from km 31 at Barasat and 398
 Km at Raiganj in West Bengal by availing assistance from Asian Development Bank.  While the total project size is around
 Rs.1085.70 crore, the outlay for the year 2004-05 is Rs.113.50 crore.  Separately, Rs.3210 crore has been earmarked for NHAI
 for Externally Aided Project out of which Rs.2568 crore is being provided as Grant and Rs.642 crore as EAP-loan.
 
14.        National Highways (Original) Works are capital works on Non-NHDP highways such as two laning, four laning,
 construction of bye-passes, construction of Rail over-Bridges, construction of Bridges, widening of roads etc. Budgetary
 provision for National Highway Works (O) for the year 2004-05 is Rs.1487 crore out of which Rs.1338.80 crore is for the
 States and Union Territories other than Sikkim and North Eastern States and a sum of Rs.148.20 crore has been earmarked for
 2004-05 for Sikkim and North Eastern States.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP) 
15.        The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways that the Government has embarked upon
 a massive programme to develop highways through the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) in the country.  The
 NHDP is the largest highway project ever undertaken in the country.  This is being implemented by NHAI.  The NHDP
 consists of Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West Corridors, Port Connectivity and other Projects.  The total length
 under NHDP is about 14,279 km.  The details relating to NHDP are as under:-
(i)
                  Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) comprising National Highways connecting four metro cities viz., Delhi, Mumbai,
 Chennai and Kolkata.  Total length of GQ is 5846 km.  As on 31 st March 2004, four-laning of 2082 km has
 already been completed and work is under various stages of implementation on the entire balance length of
 3764 km under 78 different contracts.

STATUS OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP
 
21.        The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways regarding the status of National Highways
 not covered under NHDP.  The Committee also enquired about the condition of these Highways in terms of lane width and
 quality etc.  In reply, the Committee was informed that the present total National Highway length in the country is about 65,569
 km.  This includes a total length of 7457 km of state roads, declared as new National Highways on 25.02.2004. Out of the total
 length of 65,569 km, 14279 km are being improved to 4 lanes under NHDP.  The 7457 km length of newly declared National
 Highways is yet to be handed over by the State Governments.  The balance length of National Highways is about 43,833 km.
 The details of these National Highways in terms of their lane width are as under:-
 
22.        The Committee was further informed that out of about 43,833 km of National Highways, about 10,000 km length of

24.        The Committee observes that the main objective relating to the road sector for the Tenth Plan is balanced development
 of the total network.  The task would include widening of roads, improvement in riding quality and strengthening and road
 safety measures to cater to the growing demand for road services.  However, the Committee notes with dismay that out of
 43,833 kilometer of non-NHDP National Highways, only 1.95 per cent are four or more laned whereas 62.55 per cent of such
 National Highways are two-laned and 35.49 per cent of such National Highways are only single/intermediate laned.  The
 Committee cannot accept the wishful thinking of the Ministry that "this is intended to be implemented mostly through private
 sector participation on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis" without being supported by any specific facts.  Going by the past
 records, the Committee also feels it is not suggestive that such course will be available to the Government.  The allocation
 made for these National Highways is also meagre  when compared to the allocations made for National Highways under
 NHDP.  There is a mismatch between NHDP and non-NHDP Highways in terms of lanes, surface quality and funds. 
 Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should give equitable weightage to the
 non-NHDP National Highways and provide adequate budgetary allocation required for their development as envisaged in the
 Tenth Plan.  A balanced approach should be adopted for increasing the lane width and improving the riding quality of these
 National Highways.  This will ensure that those parts of the country which are not connected with National Highways under
 NHDP also get due attention.  The development of National Highways in these areas will also help improve the economic
 development of such places.
 
VALUE ADDITION TO THE LAND ADJOINING NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
25.        During the course of the evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, the Committee
 observed that construction of National Highways results in appreciation of economic value of land on both sides of the road.  
 Hence while creating world-class roads, the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways adds value to the lands adjoining the
 roads and there is a price appreciation of these lands.  As a result, the owners of the land adjoining National Highway get
 advantage without investing any money. 
26.        The Committee feels that in view of the resource crunch being faced by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways,
 there is a genuine need for generation of additional revenue by the Ministry.  Whenever any National Highway is constructed, it
 leads to huge value addition to the land adjoining the National Highway and these benefits of addition in value have so far been
 enjoyed by private agencies only.   The Government should also get advantage of the appreciation of land value because it is
 the taxpayer's money that has led to the value addition of that property.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Government may explore the possibility of imposing some cess/tax on land adjoining National Highways which is being
 utilized for commercial purpose on annual basis.  This could serve as a permanent source of income for the Government and the
 revenue so generated could be ploughed back only for the construction and maintenance of National Highways in the country. 
 Provision of ducting at the time of construction of National Highways for laying telephone and electric cables also leads to
 value addition and can be explored for generating more funds for the road sector. These measures may go a long way to meet
 the resource gap for maintenance and construction of National Highways in the country.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS ENTRUSTED WITH BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION (BRO)
 
27.        The Border Road Organisation has been entrusted with 4704 km length of National Highways in the States of Andhra
 Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jammu & Kashmir, Maharashtra, Uttaranchal, and the North-Eastern States including Sikkim.  The

D R A F T R E P O R T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/82ndreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:03:03]
 funds for development and maintenance of these National Highways are being provided by the Ministry of Defence or the
 Ministry of Road Transport & Highways depending on the strategic requirement.
 
28.        During 2003-04, the overall allocation from Ministry of Road Transport & Highways to the BRO was Rs.256 crore for
 development and Rs.17 crore for maintenance of these National Highways. During the year 2004-05, Rs.210 crore have been
 allocated to the BRO for development and Rs.17 crore for maintenance.  A major portion of the funds amounting to Rs.110
 crore has been allocated for the North Eastern States.
           
29.        During the course of the evidence, the Committee brought to the notice of the representatives of the Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways and BRO that high-intensity explosives are being used while constructing the roads in the hilly areas. 
 This often results in landslides which lead to washing away of roads, bridges and residential areas.  The Committee sought the
 response of BRO in the matter.  Replying to the query, the representative of the BRO agreed with the view expressed by the
 Committee.  The Committee was informed that so far the executing agencies in the hilly areas were using high-intensity
 explosives.  The Committee was further informed that in view of the adverse effects of the high-intensity explosives, the
 Government of India has directed the manufacturing agencies to try for other alternatives.  The BRO was trying to switch over
 to some other system in this respect.  
 
30.        The Committee is of the opinion that hilly areas have a delicate ecological system and there is a need to reduce blasting
 in these areas so that the hill slopes do not destabilize or fall.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the BRO should
 switch over to using  low-intensity explosives while making roads in such areas.   The BRO should also consider constructing
 tunnels in hilly areas, wherever required.
 
31.        The Committee also enquired from the representatives of BRO as to whether they had any Research and Development
 facility within their own organisation to address such problems.  The Committee was informed that BRO had no specific
 Research and Development facility available with them.  However, it was mentioned that BRO had a huge experience of over
 forty years in road construction in hilly areas.
 
32.        The Committee is aware that Border Roads Organisation is a well disciplined, motivated construction organisation in
 the country equipped with proven capability and expertise developed over more than forty years in the area of construction of
 roads, national highways, permanent bridges etc. in the border and hilly areas.  However, the Committee is surprised to know
 that no Research and Development facility is available in the BRO.  The Committee is of the opinion that R&D should be an
 integral part of any organisation working in a field where technological advancements are bound to take place.  Practical
 experience of BRO of making roads in hilly areas is no doubt an added advantage for them but having an institutional
 mechanism for research and development is absolutely essential in the contemporary age.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the BRO should develop a Research and Development facility of their own so that they can have access to the
 modern technology and they could stay in touch with technological advancements in the field of making roads on hilly areas. 
 
DEVELOPMENT OF NEWLY DECLARED NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
33.        From a perusal of the documents submitted by Ministry of Road Transport & Highways for examination of Demands
 for Grants of that Ministry, the Committee observed that 7457 km of state road in various states had been declared as new
 National Highways on 25
th February 2004.  However, the newly declared lengths of National Highways were yet to be handed
 over to the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways by the State Governments.  In this context, the Secretary of the Ministry,
 during the course of the evidence, stated as under:-
 
"The total range of 7457 km of state roads were declared National Highways and those roads are yet to be handed over
 to us by the State Government.  The procedure is, the State Government makes a request.  We do not take over on our
 own.  The State Government requests and then we take it over.  So far roads have not been handed over".
           
34.        The Committee is concerned to note that certain lengths of state roads had not been handed over to the Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways for taking over the roads for development even after a period of nearly six months after their declaration
 as National Highways.  The Committee feels that once the roads are declared as National Highways, the physical possession of
 the roads should be immediately taken over by the central agencies for their development as National Highways.  The
 Committee recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should adopt a proactive approach in this regard. 
 Before declaring a state road as National Highway, such lengths of the road must fulfil the criterion for declaration as National
 Highway.  The guidelines for declaration of state roads as National Highways should also be so revised that the State
 Governments fulfil the required criterion before any road is declared as National Highway.

 additional fund due to this additional cess.  The matter has already been taken up with the Ministry of Finance at various levels

 for release of additional cess as per the CRF Act, 2000.

ROAD SAFETY
47.        Road Safety is a area of serious concern.  An allocation of Rs.29.00 crore was made for this sector in BE 2003-2004
 which was reduced to Rs.28.16 crore at the RE stage.  However, the actual expenditure during the year was to the tune of
 Rs.28.24 crore.  Now an amount of      Rs.33.20 crore has been allocated in BE 2004-05.  Under this scheme, a number of
 activities such as publicity and awareness campaign on road safety, grants-in-aid to Non Governmental Organisations (NGOs)
 to create awareness on road safety/administer road safety programmes, assistance in the form of equipment for accident relief
 and refresher training to drivers in the unorganized sector are being undertaken.
           
48.        The Committee brought to the notice of the Ministry that in recent year, more than 80,000 persons had been killed in
 accidents on Indian roads annually.  The Committee further pointed out that the Delhi-Jaipur and Delhi-Agra Highways were
 the most accident prone of the five highways leading out of Delhi.  The Committee enquired as to whether Ministry of Road
 Transport & Highways had conducted any survey to identify the factors which have been the cause of higher rate of accidents
 on the two highways and taken remedial measures. 
 
49.        In response, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways that a study had been
 conducted by a private consultant for the NHAI to identify the requirement of improvements related to road safety on NH-2
 (Delhi-Agra section) and NH-8 (Delhi-Jaipur section).  The consultant has suggested some of the remedial measures for
 enhancing the road safety on these two highways such as road markings, delineators, road signs, improvement of junctions,
 improvement of median openings, provision of service road etc.  The total estimated cost of these works as submitted by the
 consultant is Rs.121.22 crore.  The reports are being scrutinized and further action for execution of these works will be taken
 thereafter keeping in view the availability of the resources.   The Committee enquired from the Ministry regarding the steps
 taken for increasing public awareness about road safety.  In response, the Committee was informed that the Ministry works
 with the different State Governments and NGOs in the following areas:-
·
               refresher training for heavy vehicle drivers
·               evacuation of accident victims from the accident spot to the nearest hospital by assisting States and NGOs with
 ambulances
·               removal of vehicles involved in accidents on National Highways by providing a crane to States and NGOs
·               checking overloading of vehicles
·               NGOs and institutions are also given financial assistance for conducting refresher training to drivers of heavy
 commercial vehicles in the unorganized sector
·               providing non-recurring financial assistance to State Government / NGOs for setting up model driver training
 schools.
·               publicity and awareness on road safety through campaigns in print and electronic media.
50.        The Committee observes that the mortality rate due to the road accidents in the country is too high.  The rate of
 accidents has gone up after the improvement in the riding quality of our highways.  The Committee feels that so far the
 measures taken by the Government to contain road accidents have proved to be inadequate.  Hence there is an urgent need to
 re-devise the strategy for taking remedial measures and minimize road accidents.  The Committee recommends that the
 Government should introduce road safety devices and launch awareness programmes for the public and transport users in a big
 way.  The Committee takes note that a consultant has suggested some remedial measures for enhancing the road safety on some
 highways.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should adopt a proactive
 approach in this regard and there should be wider and effective use of fast improving applications of information technology
 and communication technology to monitor technical deficiencies on the roads.  The Committee suggests that the Ministry of
 Road Transport & Highways should involve their R&D wing and before constructing National Highways, road safety features
 should be incorporated in the design of the road at the detailed project report stage itself. 
 
51.        During the course of the evidence, the Committee observed that there had been frequent digging of National Highways
 by various local and central agencies.  This exercise is mostly undertaken for laying of cables etc.  However, the roads are not
 laid properly after that and are merely filled up with mud.  In some cases the process goes on in a very haphazard way.  Such
 portions of the road sink inside during rains.  The drivers of the vehicles passing through the roads are not aware of the puddles
 and the potholes so created.  This often leads to serious accidents which result in loss of precious lives and property.
           
52.        The Committee is of the view that with the development and improvement in riding quality of the roads in the country,

DIFFERENTIAL PRICING SYSTEM FOR PRIVATE VEHICLES
59.        During the course of the oral evidence, the Committee observed that the automobile population in the country had been

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
AT A GLANCE
 
PLAN PROVISIONS
According to the Tenth Five Year Plan, roads are the key to the development of an economy.  However, the allocations
 made for the road sector do not indicate their importance in the economic development of the country.  The Committee notes
 with concern that there is a huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during the Tenth Plan.  A good
 road network constitutes the basic infrastructure that propels the development process through connectivity and opening up the
 backward regions to trade and investment.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to achieve the objective of
 Tenth Plan in road sector, the budget allocation of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  The Committee notes that the Government has not been able to attract private investment as anticipated.  Therefore,
 the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan so as to
 reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent. 
(Para 10)
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
The Committee notes that about 90% of the Golden Quadrilateral is proposed to be completed by December 2004.  The
 Committee recommends that the Government should take all necessary steps to make sure that the works proposed to be
 completed by December 2004 are completed within that period.  However, the Committee is not satisfied with the reasons
 given by the Ministry for delay in completion of NHDP programme.  The reasons are general in nature and could have been
 anticipated well in advance whereby the time of one year could have been saved.  This clearly shows the lack of proactive
 approach on the part of the Ministry. The Committee also recommends that the Government should evolve a monitoring
 mechanism to ensure quality of construction, making officials accountable for failure, transparency in implementation process,
 penalising defaulting contractors etc. so that the remaining part of the project is also completed within the revised targeted
 period.
(Para 20)
STATUS OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP
The Committee observes that the main objective relating to the road sector for the Tenth Plan is balanced development
 of the total network.  The task would include widening of roads, improvement in riding quality and strengthening and road
 safety measures to cater to the growing demand for road services.  However, the Committee notes with dismay that out of
 43,833 kilometer of non-NHDP National Highways, only 1.95 per cent are four or more laned whereas 62.55 per cent of such
 National Highways are two-laned and 35.49 per cent of such National Highways are only single/intermediate laned.  The
 Committee cannot accept the wishful thinking of the Ministry that "this is intended to be implemented mostly through private
 sector participation on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis" without being supported by any specific facts.  Going by the past
 records, the Committee also feels it is not suggestive that such course will be available to the Government.  The allocation
 made for these National Highways is also meagre  when compared to the allocations made for National Highways under
 NHDP.  There is a mismatch between NHDP and non-NHDP Highways in terms of lanes, surface quality and funds. 
 Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should give equitable weightage to the
 non-NHDP National Highways and provide adequate budgetary allocation required for their development as envisaged in the
 Tenth Plan.  A balanced approach should be adopted for increasing the lane width and improving the riding quality of these
 National Highways.  This will ensure that those parts of the country which are not connected with National Highways under
 NHDP also get due attention.  The development of National Highways in these areas will also help improve the economic
 development of such places.
(Para 24)
VALUE ADDITION TO THE LAND ADJOINING NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
The Committee feels that in view of the resource crunch being faced by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways,
 there is a genuine need for generation of additional revenue by the Ministry.  Whenever any National Highway is constructed, it
 leads to huge value addition to the land adjoining the National Highway and these benefits of addition in value have so far been
 enjoyed by private agencies only.   The Government should also get advantage of the appreciation of land value because it is
 the taxpayer's money that has led to the value addition of that property.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Government may explore the possibility of imposing some cess/tax on land adjoining National Highways which is being
 utilized for commercial purpose on annual basis.  This could serve as a permanent source of income for the Government and the
 revenue so generated could be ploughed back only for the construction and maintenance of National Highways in the country.

 note that at a time when, during the 10
th Plan, the road transport sector is faced with a resource gap of over Rs.1,00,000 crore,
 the Ministry has not been able to prioritise its programmes.  The Committee feels that through a Government regulation, the
 Government is forcing the people in the country to switch over to the much expensive HSRP.  The Committee is not able to
 understand the reasons which necessitated the Government to make a compulsory financial burden on the people by introducing
 the HSRP.  Though the Government has no indication to have single technology provider, however, the Committee has
 apprehension that given the specifications of HSRP, there is very likelihood of monopolistic regime deciding the course of
 development in the matter.  The Committee further recommends that given the development of the information technology and
 its induction in this sector, the Government should have focused attention on capacity building towards the choice of the
 appropriate technology-model and encourage the emergence and promotion of multiple players.  

D R A F T R E P O R T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/82ndreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:03:03]
 (Para 45)
ROAD SAFETY
The Committee observes that the mortality rate due to the road accidents in the country is too high.  The rate of
 accidents has gone up after the improvement in the riding quality of our highways.  The Committee feels that so far the
 measures taken by the Government to contain road accidents have proved to be inadequate.  Hence there is an urgent need to
 re-devise the strategy for taking remedial measures and minimize road accidents.  The Committee recommends that the
 Government should introduce road safety devices and launch awareness programmes for the public and transport users in a big
 way.  The Committee takes note that a consultant has suggested some remedial measures for enhancing the road safety on some
 highways.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should adopt a proactive
 approach in this regard and there should be wider and effective use of fast improving applications of information technology
 and communication technology to monitor technical deficiencies on the roads.  The Committee suggests that the Ministry of
 Road Transport & Highways should involve their R&D wing and before constructing National Highways, road safety features
 should be incorporated in the design of the road at the detailed project report stage itself. 
(Para 50)
The Committee is of the view that with the development and improvement in riding quality of the roads in the country,
 the speed of the vehicles has also gone up.  Non-uniformity of the quality of the surface because of indiscriminate digging and
 non-compliance of rules by other departments while digging, presence of slow moving vehicles particularly in densely
 populated areas, straying of animals in the carriageways lead to fatal accidents.  Therefore, the Committee feels that availability
 of service roads/underpasses in densely populated areas is of immense importance.  The Committee further feels that laying
 ducts is not only beneficial for value addition and resource mobilization but also for avoiding indiscriminate digging.  The
 Committee is of the view that lack of telecommunication facility on the National Highways is also responsible for higher death
 rate.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should ensure the availability of adequate
 telecommunication for availing medical facility.  The Committee further recommends that in view of the growing number of
 accidents, adequately equipped trauma centers should be opened at reasonable distances on National Highways.
            (Para 52)
           
The Committee is of the view that if ever the roads are required to be dug up, they must be restored to their earlier
 position.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways should make it mandatory
 that the quality of National Highways should be restored by the authority undertaking the digging work to a workable condition
 so as to be able to cope up with the traffic load till repair work is undertaken by the NHAI or concerned PWD.  The violators in
 this respect should be punished adequately. 
Para 54)
MODEL DRIVER TRAINING SCHOOL
The Committee also notes that in the recent past, there have been a large number of cases of accidents involving school
 buses wherein a number of school children have lost lives or suffered grievous injuries.  The Committee is of the opinion that in
 view of the high rate of accidents due to the fault of the drivers, it is extremely essential that driver training schools are set up in
 as much states as possible.  However, the Committee feels that this is one area where instead of asking for additional funds, the
 Government should attempt to invite private sector investment.  The Government should concentrate more on regulating the
 quality of training in driving skill being imparted by these schools.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Government should make efforts to attract private sector investment in the opening of more and more driver training schools in
 the country.  The Committee is also of the view that unskilled drivers with licenses are like doctors with fake degrees and both
 are equally dangerous to the society.  The Committee is of the view that a substantial number of drivers are getting licenses
 using unscrupulous means with the connivance of corrupt officials.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the
 Government should suggest all license issuing authorities to have stringent norms for issuing license to the drivers. 
(Para 58)
DIFFERENTIAL PRICING SYSTEM FOR PRIVATE VEHICLES
During the course of the oral evidence, the Committee observed that the automobile population in the country had been
 growing disproportionately with respect to the infrastructure created and the roads were under undue pressure.  In view, the
 Committee was of the opinion that there was a need to adopt a policy which discourages owning of multiple vehicles.  The
 efforts of the Government should focus on developing the public transport.  In order to discourage owning multiple vehicles,
 the Government should adopt a methodology whereby the rich and the affluent are asked to pay more for keeping more than
 one vehicle.  Acquiring more than one vehicle in a family should invite financial disincentives.  This would certainly
 discourage owning of multiple vehicles.  Further, it would also help release the pressure on the surface of the roads and also

 help positively to reduce vehicular pollution.
(Para 59)
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to undertake studies with regard to modernization and capacity
 building of road transport sector in the country with respect to its present and future scenario. The Committee is in agreement
 with the view expressed by the Secretary with regard to the inadequacy of the allocation for Research and Development
 activities of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the allocation for
 Research and Development should be adequately increased at RE stage.

REPORT
 
The Commission of Railway Safety deals with matters pertaining to safety in rail travel and operation.  For
 discharge of these functions, the Commission derives certain statutory powers from the Railways Act, 1989 and the
 rules framed thereunder.  While the Railway Board in the Ministry of Railways are the safety controlling authority and
 are responsible for laying down and enforcing safety standards for the Indian Railways, the main task of the
 Commission is to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation, inspection, audit,
 investigatory and advisory functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard
 to the soundness of rail construction and safety in train operation.  The most crucial function of the Commission of
 Railway Safety is to ensure that any new Railway line to be opened for passenger traffic should conform to the
 standards and specifications prescribed by the Ministry of Railways and the new line is safe in all respects for carrying
 of passenger traffic.  Similar job is also performed in respect of other works such as gauge conversion, doubling of lines
 and electrification of existing lines.  Another important function of the Commission is to conduct statutory inquiry into
 serious train accidents occurring on the Indian Railways and to make recommendations for improving Railway Safety.  
 
2.         Since Railway safety is of paramount importance to all and the fact that there had been a spurt in train accidents
 during the recent past, the Committee decided to study the functioning of Commission of Railway Safety.  Since the
 Commission of Railway Safety is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee
 asked the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish a status note on the functioning of Commission of Railway Safety for its
 consideration. 
 
3.         In the status note submitted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Committee was informed about the genesis of
 the Commission of Railway Safety.  It was brought out that formerly the Commission of Railway Safety was called the
 Railway Inspectorate and it functioned under the control of the Railway Board till May 1941. In the wake of a serious
 accident in 1937, the Central Legislature considered that the Commission, which was charged with the responsibility
 for conducting inquires into serious railway accidents as also for the inspection of Railways, should not function under
 the administrative control of the same executive authority whose work it was required to inspect and comment upon. 
 The principle of separation of the Railway Inspectorate from the Railway Board was endorsed in 1940 by the Central
 Legislature who recommended that "Senior Government Inspectors of Railways should be placed under the
 Administrative control of some authority of the Government of India other than the Railway Board."  The Railway
 Inspectorate was then separated from the control of Railway Board to secure its independence from the authority
 administering the Railways.  After its separation, the Railway Inspectorate was placed under the administrative control
 of the then Department of Communications with effect from 12
th May 1941.  On 9 th July 1942, this Department of
 Communication was bifurcated into two Departments viz (i) Post & Air Department and (ii) War Transport
 Department.  The Railway Inspectorate was kept under the administrative control of Posts & Air Department and
 continuously thereafter under whichever Ministry that held the portfolio of Civil Aviation.  It was re-designated as the
 Commission of Railway Safety on 1.11.1961.  It came under the administrative control of the Ministry of Tourism and
 Civil Aviation in May 1967 subsequently re-designated as the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
ORGANISATIONAL SET UP & JURISDICTION
4.         The Commission is headed by the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety (pay scale Rs.24050-26000), who is

83rd report of Committee on Transport,Tourism and Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 also the Principal Technical Adviser to the Government of India in all matters concerning the Commission.  The
 headquarters of the Commission is located at Lucknow.  The Chief Commissioner directs the technical activities of the
 Commission and issues instruction for the guidance of Commissioners of Railway Safety in respect of holding statutory
 inquiries into serious railway accidents, inspection of new lines including electrification of existing lines prior to their
 opening for public carriage of passengers, and sanction for running of new locomotives/rolling stock.  He also co-
ordinates the work of the Commissioners in their dealings with the Railway Board and the Railway Administration.   He
 communicates his views whenever necessary to the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) on design, standards,
 specifications and procedures for construction, working and maintenance of assets in all branches of railway
 engineering and operation including civil, mechanical, electrical and signal engineering etc.  The Chief Commissioner
 is assisted by a Deputy Commissioner of Railway Safety (General) (pay scale Rs.14300-18300).  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety is assisted by a regular section of Ministry of Civil Aviation under a Section Officer
 who reports to Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Civil Aviation as well as Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 5.         There is a Technical Wing attached to the Chief Commissioner at his headquarters which has four Deputy
 Commissioners of Railway Safety (pay scale Rs.12000-16500) drawn from the mechanical, electrical, signaling,
 telecommunication and operating disciplines of Indian Railways.  The Technical Wing has two posts of Technical
 Assistant (pay scale Rs.4500-7000), two LDC, three stenographers and few group 'D' staff.  The Technical Wing has a
 post of Assistant Director (Official Language) (pay scale Rs.6500-10500).
 
6.         Working under the administrative control of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety are nine Commissioners of
 Railway Safety (pay scale Rs.22400-24500), each one exercising jurisdiction over one of the 9 Zonal Railways, two
 with headquarters at Mumbai, 3 with headquarters at Kolkata and one each with headquarters at Bangalore, New Delhi,
 Lucknow and Secunderabad.  In addition, some of their jurisdictions cover railway establishments falling under their
 jurisdiction viz Metro Railway, Kolkata, DMRC, Delhi, MRTP, Chennai and Konkan Railway.  There are two Deputy
 Commissioners of Railway Safety (Signalling and Telecommunication) (pay scale Rs.12000-16500) headquartered at
 Mumbai and Kolkata.  Each Commissioner is an independent statutory authority under the Railway Act, 1989.  Each
 Commissioner of Railway Safety is assisted by a bare minimum staff of a stenographer/Sr. Private Secretary, one
 Office Superintendent (pay scale Rs.5500-9000), one Safety Assistant (pay scale Rs.5000-8000), one/two UDCs, one to
 four LDCs and a few Group 'D' staff.
 
APPOINTMENT TO THE CADRE OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
7.         The Deputy Commissioners of Railway Safety are appointed on deputation/absorption from the applicants drawn
 from Signaling, Electrical, Mechanical, Operating and Civil Engineering Departments of Indian Railways.  The period
 of deputation as per extant recruitment rules is five years.  During the period of deputation the officers are entitled to
 deputation allowance as per the instructions of Ministry of Finance.  However, in their case the restriction that pay plus
 deputation allowance shall not exceed the maximum of scale has been relaxed.  The officers are governed by Railway
 TA rules and are eligible for free passes and Privilege Ticket Orders (PTOs) on the same lines as other Railway
 Officers of corresponding status. 
 
8.         The Commissioners of Railway Safety are selected by the Union Public Service Commission on absorption basis
 from amongst the applicants who are senior officers drawn from Civil Engineering Department of the Indian Railways
 and once confirmed cannot return back to railway service, but are governed by Railway TA rules and are eligible for
 free passes and PTOs on the same lines as other Railway Officers of corresponding status. 
 
9.         The Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety is selected by the Union Public Service Commission from amongst
 the existing Commissioners who have put in a minimum of three years of service in the grade.
 
10.       The supporting staff of the Commission is appointed in the Commission itself through Employment Exchange
 and Staff Selection Commission etc. and are governed by civil rules for TA etc. and are not entitled for free passes and
 PTOs.
FUNCTIONS
11.       The responsibility for safety in the working and operation of Railway rests solely with Railway Board and the
 Zonal Railway authorities.  The main task of the Commission of Railway Safety is to direct, advise and caution the

83rd report of Committee on Transport,Tourism and Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 Railway executives with a view to ensure that all reasonable precautions are taken in regard to soundness of rail
 construction and safety of train operation.  The Railway Board refers to the Commission matters relating to
 modification or enhancement of standards in respect of operation of trains, track, locomotive, rolling stock and revision
 of rules embodied in the General Rules, Rules for the opening of New Lines, Manuals, IRCA Regulations, Schedules of
 Dimensions and other publications.  Suggestions made by the Commission of Railway Safety are duly considered by
 the Railway Board before necessary revisions are notified.
 
12.       The duties and functions of the Commissioners are laid down in the Railways Act, 1989 and rules framed
 thereunder, and executive instructions issued from time to time.  These are briefly:
·
              to conduct statutory inquires into serious railway accidents and suggest safeguards.
·              to inspect new railway lines with a view to determining whether they are fit to be opened for the
 public carriage of passenger, and to sanction their opening after inspection on behalf of the Central
 Government.
·              to sanction the execution of all new works and installations on the running track affecting the
 safety of the traveling public such as rebuilding of bridges, remodeling of station yards, line
 capacity works, resignalling works, etc.
·              to make periodical inspections of railways and report to the Central Government on any condition
 which may endanger the safety of the traveling public and make recommendations.
·              to examine the technical aspects of new rolling stock and advise on their sanctions and increase in
 speeds.
·              to authorize the carriage of oversized consignments stipulating the conditions for their movements.
·              to recommend and sanction infringements to the schedule of dimensions prescribed by the
 Government of India.
·              to grant dispensation from general rules under approved special instructions subject to stipulated
 safeguards.
·              to oversee the accident prevention efficacy of the zonal railway administrations by reviewing the
 reports of departmental enquiries into less serious accidents.
 
13.       Field duties of the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety consist of inspections of sections of Railways, visits
 to the Railway Headquarters and Divisional Offices, Railway installations and Circle Offices.  If considered necessary
 by him, he may himself hold inquiries into important accidents.   The Chief Commissioner submits an annual report on
 the working of the Commission which is laid on the table of both the Houses of Parliament.
 
14.       The Committee took the oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Chief Commissioner of
 Railway Safety at its meeting held on the 20
th May 2003 to get an indepth insight into the functions of the Commission
 and to discuss the essential aspects of the working of the Commission.  On the basis of the information furnished by the
 Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, the Committee also elicited the views
 of the Chairman, Railway Board on the subject at its meeting held on the 14th July 2003.  In order to get wider views on
 the subject, the Committee, at its meeting held on the 4 th September 2003, decided to invite the views of individuals
 and institutions interested in the subject through advertisement in all major national dailies and vernacular newspapers
 all over the country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda
 on various aspects of the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety from a lot of people including many retired
 Commissioners/Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.
 
15.       The issues pointed out by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Commission of Railway Safety, the response of
 the Ministry of Railways thereon and the observations/recommendations of the Committee have been discussed in the
 succeeding paragraphs.
 
ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
16.       The Committee observed that the Commission of Railway Safety had been working under the administrative
 control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Committee enquired from the Commission of Railway Safety as to whether

83rd report of Committee on Transport,Tourism and Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/83rdreport.htm[22-10-2018 12:04:05]
 the present arrangement of the Commission working under the Ministry of Civil Aviation was satisfactory or whether
 there were any difficulties in the existing arrangement.  The Committee also sought suggestion of Chief Commissioner
 of Railway Safety to make the working of the Commission more effective.   The Committee was informed that the
 Commission of Railway Safety is a high level statutory body charged with the responsibility for the inspection of new
 railway lines prior to their opening for passenger traffic, inspection of open lines, inquiries into serious Railway
 Accidents, and certain other duties connected with safety of railway operation as required under the Railways Act
 1989.  The Committee was also informed by the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety that during the course of
 working as Commissioners, they are required to take tough stands against the Railways and their working in many
 cases and hence it will not be in the interest of the impartial working of the Commission to keep it attached with the
 Ministry of Railways.  It is because of the independence the Commission enjoys from the Ministry of Railways that
 they are able to discharge their duties impartially.  In response to the query as to whether the Commission of Railway
 Safety should remain with the Ministry of Civil Aviation or should it be attached to any other organization, other than
 Ministry of Railways, Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety stated that for the past more than 50 years, the
 Commission of Railway Safety has been attached with that Ministry which deals with Civil Aviation.  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety stated that the Commission could as well be attached, with any other Ministry.  The
 Committee was further informed that the question regarding the Ministry under which the Commission of Railway
 Safety should function was considered by three high level Railway Accident Committees:
 
·
        Railway Accident Committee 1962 (Kunzru Committee )
·        Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee 1968 (Wanchoo Committee)
·        Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee 1978 (Sikri Committee)
 
17.       All these Committees went into great depth and after considering their recommendations, the Government every
 time decided that the Commission of Railway Safety should not be with the Ministry of Railways but remain outside it
 and decided to keep the Commission of Railway Safety under the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Appointments
 Committee of the Cabinet re-considered this issue in 1998 and decided to maintain status quo i.e. to keep Commission
 of Railway Safety under administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 
18.       As regard the suggestion to make the working of the Commission more effective, the Chief Commissioner of
 Railway Safety was of the view that the Commission should enjoy the autonomy as available with the Election
 Commission, Central Vigilance Commission, Union Public Service Commission or Comptroller and Auditor General. 
 In that event the Commissioners of Railway Safety will be able to assert themselves in ensuring that their
 recommendations and observations are enforceable and do not remain merely recommendatory.  The Commission
 needs to be given active support and assistance in the pursuit of its objectives.  Also the budget provisions for the
 Commission of Railway Safety should be delinked from the budget of Ministry of Civil Aviation and it should be on
 the lines of other autonomous bodies like Election Commission, Union Public Service Commission, Central Vigilance
 Commission, or Comptroller and Auditor General.
           
19.       During the evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Railways, the Committee sought the opinion of the
 Chairman, Railway Board as to whether the Commission of Railway Safety should be an independent body like the
 Election Commission of India.  The Chairman, Railway Board opined as under:-
 
"Sir, I personally feel that we should maintain the creditability of the Deputy Chief Commissioners of Railway
 Safety.  The general public still feels that they are under the Ministry of Railway; it may be directly or
 indirectly.  I personally feel that it should be an independent body.  I fully agree with you. ……. It will

 provided, the following are ensured through introduction of provisions in the relevant Act and Rules:-
A clause should be included in the relevant laws that no railway servant can be prosecuted without the sanction
 of the authority competent to appoint him or a higher authority.   Further, it should be stipulated that the

 need to be extended to Commissioner of Railway Safety.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation has agreed with these

 by many retired Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.  It was brought out that the Commission of Railway Safety
 cannot prevent interference by the police in the smooth conducting of the enquiry.  Very often the police try to seize
 documents and other evidence relating to the accident, on the grounds that an act of criminal negligence had been
 committed and they had registered a criminal case.  Such action of the police affects the Commissioner of Railway
 Safety's enquiry.  Very often the Commissioner of Railway Safety is reduced to having to plead with higher officials in

 enquiries in camera and not hold them as public enquiries.  This is because the proceedings do not enjoy the privileges
 of a judicial enquiry, and are not protected by provisions such as contempt action.  This leaves ground for interested
 parties and the media to provide false or prejudiced reports about the enquiry. 
 
47.       The comments of the Ministry of Railways were sought in the matter.  The Ministry of Railways informed the
 Committee that Section 186 of the Railways Act, 1989 provides that no suit, prosecution and other legal proceedings
 shall lie against the Central Government, any railway administration, a railway servant or any other person for anything

 which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act or any rules or orders made there under. 
 Section 8 of the Railways Act, 1989 further provides that the Commissioner of Railway Safety shall be deemed to be a
 public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.  From the perusal of the said provisions it
 appears that the Commissioner of Railway Safety is fully protected from being prosecuted or being used for anything
 which he has done in good faith or intended to do in pursuance of the Railways Act or any rules/orders made
 thereunder.
           
48.       As far as the question of the Commissioner of Railway Safety or any investigating authority should not be called
 as witness or for examination by any court, is concerned, this power of the court flows from the Code of Criminal
 Procedure and Code of Civil Procedure.  The Court is free to summon any person to give evidence in any case pending
 before it.
 
49.       Article 361 of the Constitution of India provides that the President or Governor of a State shall not be
 answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers/duties of his officers or for any act done or
 purposed to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties.
           
50.       Under Section 121 of the Indian Evidence Act, it has been provided that no judge or magistrate shall be
 compelled to answer questions as to (a) his conduct in court as such judge or magistrate; or (b) anything which came to
 his knowledge in court as such judge or magistrate except upon an order of the court to which he is subordinate.
           
51.       In accordance with the provisions of the Evidence Act, even the judge or magistrate is not exempted from being
 called as a witness in a court of law.  Section 133 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for exempting of certain
 persons from personal appearance in a court of law.  There is a provision that if any witness is not able to come to
 court, his statement can be recorded in the commission.  The fact remains that the judge of a civil court can also be
 called as a witness to testify any fact.  Only exception to this rule are the provisions of Article 361 of the Constitution. 
 The Commissioner of Railway Safety does not fit into this exception.  He is deemed to be a public servant within the
 meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.  He is only entitled to the privileges which are available to a public
 servant under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
 
52.       The Committee is constrained to note that the inquiry reports of the Commission of Railway Safety on accidents

 is in agreement with the recommendations made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998, quoted at para 43 above.

 amended at the earliest.  The Committee also recommends that when the Commission of Railway Safety proposes to
 take up an inquiry, inquiries initiated by police or magistrate should be stopped and the civil and police authorities

 by the Committee will enable the Commissioners of Railway Safety in undertaking their inquiries without any
 hindrances.  Thereby, the inquiry reports of the Commissioners on accidents could also be published as soon as the
 inquiry is over and the public at large would not be deprived of their vital right to information.

 Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety was given an additional 2 years, enabling him to retire at 60 years.  Now, both
 the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety and the Commissioners retired at the age of 60 years. 
 
60.       The Committee is constrained to note that vacancies continue to exist in the Commission of Railway Safety for
 fairly long periods because of non-availability of eligible officers from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee
 recommends that any vacancy arising in the Commission of Railway Safety should be filled up at the earliest so that the
 functioning of the Commission does not suffer.  The Committee is also constrained to note that the recommendations
 made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 are yet to be implemented by the Government.  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety, being the Principal Technical Advisor to the Government of India on matters
 concerning rail safety, is the highest technical official in the Ministry of Civil Aviation for dealing with railway safety. 
 The Committee is of the view that upgradation of the post of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety to the level of
 Secretary to the Government of India is absolutely essential so that he can effectively and forcefully interact with the
 nine Secretary level officers of Railway Board.  Lack of such a status to the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 works as a serious deterrent to him in discharging his duties effectively in a hierarchy conscious bureaucracy.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the status of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety should be equal to that of
 the Chairman of Railway Board in rank and pay.  Likewise the status of Commissioner of Railway Safety should be
 equal to that of General Manager of a Zonal Railway in rank as well as pay.  The posts of Deputy Commissioners of
 Railway Safety should be manned by Senior Administration Grade Officers.   The Commissioners of Railway Safety
 should also be provided with the assistance of Deputy Commissioners. The Committee further recommends that, as
 recommended by the Fifth Central Pay Commission, the tenure of the Chief Commissioner should be five years, taking
 him beyond normal retirement age and upto 62 years.  The Committee is of the firm view that these measures would
 bring to an end the current scenario of shortage of volunteers opting to join the Commission of Railway Safety.   Also
 these measures will significantly enhance the status of the Commission, make it more dynamic and enable it to
 discharge its functions more effectively and its views heard and acted upon, with due importance by Railway
 Administration.
 
EXPOSURE TO TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCEMENTS
61.       The Committee pointed out that a lot of technological advancements had been taking place in the railway sector
 and enquired as to how the officers of the Commissioner kept updating their technical know-how.  In response, the
 Committee was informed by the Commission of Railway Safety that while the railways were advancing in technology
 on rolling stock, locomotives, coaches, wagons, signaling systems and railway officers were frequently sent abroad to
 visit and get a first hand knowledge of the latest technologies in the working of the railways.  However, the officers of
 the Commission do not get an equal opportunity to get exposed to the technologies which were developing abroad.  The
 Committee was also informed that Railway Board has given its officers the facility to become members of five
 professional institutions including two foreign institutions.  Again, no such facilities were available to the officers of
 Commission of Railway Safety.  The Committee was also informed that the requests of the Commission to the Railway
 Board that whenever officers of the Railways are nominated for such exposure to new technologies by sending them
 abroad, the Railway Board should also include officers of the Commission in such visits, had not been acceded to by
 the Railway Board.
 
62.       The Committee brought the above point to the notice of Railway Board and sought their comments in the
 matter.  In reply, the Committee was informed by the Railway Board that the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 had requested Ministry of Railways for training of his personnel in technology familiarization programmes abroad,
 alongwith other Indian Railway officers at Railways' cost.  The issue was examined and it was felt that dependence of
 the Commission on the Ministry of Railways for financial assistance will impair the independent identity of the
 Commission, and to maintain it, it is desirable that the Commission should be financially independent of Railways.  It
 would, therefore, not be possible to sponsor personnel of Commission of Railway Safety for training and technology
 familiarization programmes abroad on Railway expenses.

63.       The Committee feels that there is a genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed
 to the latest technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad.  Otherwise there is a
 real danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the Commission will get obsolete.  The Committee
 recommends that the officers of the Commission should be exposed to latest technologies through trainings in the
 country and abroad, so that they are in a position to perform their role effectively.  The officers of the Commission
 should also be given full facilities to become members of professional institutions, at par with the facilities extended by
 the railway administration to railway officers.  This will help in keeping the officers of the Commission updated in their
 technical knowledge.  However, for this purpose, the Commission should not depend upon the financial assistance of
 the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the budget of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is suitably increased so that these requirements could be taken care of by the
 Commission itself.
 
SUPPLY OF RAILWAY CIRCULARS ETC. TO COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
64.       During the course of the evidence of the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation and Commission of Railway
 Safety, the Committee was also informed that the Commission had to be aware of the happenings in the railway. 
 However, the Commission was not even on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board for orders/circulars affecting
 railway safety.  The Committee was further informed that the Ministry of Railways does not keep the Commission
 informed of the proceedings of various technical Committees such as Rolling Stock Committee, Signal Committee,
 Bridge Committee etc. since these Committees discuss various maintenance and safety problems encountered in day-to-
day working of the Railways.  The Commission was of the view that it would help the Commission in understanding the
 problems and steps taken to solve these problems by the Railways.  The Committee sought the comments of the
 Ministry of Railways in the above issues raised by the Commission of Railway Safety.
 
65.       Ministry of Railways informed the Committee that the Commissioner of Railway Safety is on the permanent
 mailing list of the Railway Board for all orders/circulars affecting railway safety.  As a matter of fact, copies of not
 only orders/circulars on safety, but all important policy instructions/orders/circulars etc. are endorsed to Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety.  Most of the recommendations of the Commission are generally accepted and
 instructions are issued, based on these accepted recommendations and information is given to the Commission of
 Railway Safety, regarding these instructions.
 
 
 
66.       As regards keeping the Commission informed of the proceedings of the various technical Committees, the
 Ministry of Railways replied that the various technical committees such as Rolling Stock Committee, Signal Committee
 etc. are internal Committees of the Railways to discuss various issues pertaining to the existing standards of the
 equipment of the concerned department i.e. Mechanical, Signal etc. and needs for their modifications.  Since the matter
 is totally technical pertaining to Signal and Mechanical Departments, etc. it shall be of no use to Commission as the
 proceedings of these committees are recommendatory in nature.  The recommendations made by these committees are
 examined in Board's Office, and if found suitable, only then policy instructions/guidelines are issued and the copies of
 such guidelines/instructions are also endorsed to Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 
67.       The Committee is of the view that unless the Commission of Railway Safety is kept aware of the latest
 instructions with respect to railway safety issued by the Railway Board or Zonal Railways, it cannot discharge its duties
 effectively.  Ministry of Railways have admitted that copies of all important policy orders are endorsed to the Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways should ensure that
 Commission of Railway Safety is on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board and Zonal Railways for all policy
 Circulars having bearing on safety and all Circulars/Orders affecting safety.  The Committee further recommends that
 the Commission of Railway Safety should be supplied with the proceeding of the Technical Committees of Railway
 Board so that the Commission remains informed of the safety problems encountered in the working of the railways and
 the measures taken to solve these problems.
 
LACK OF OFFICE INFRASTRUCTURE
68.       The Committee enquired from the Commission of Railway Safety regarding the budget allocation of the

 Commission and the office infrastructure available to it.  The Committee was informed that the overall budget
 allocation of the Commission has been satisfactory.  However taking into account the nature of work of Commissioner
 of Railway Safety, the allocations of funds for domestic travel as well as foreign travel has been totally inadequate. 
 The Commission of Railway Safety as well as Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety are required to be present at the
 accident site at the earliest for which they require air journey which is not possible in the present budget allocation. 
 They are also required to travel to Lucknow and Delhi in connection with discussions and conferences with Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety and RDSO at Lucknow and Railway Board and Ministry of Civil Aviation at Delhi. 
 Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety is also required to undertake extensive tours to various Zonal Railways and
 headquarters of Commissioners spread over the country in the course of discharge of his duties.  The Committee was
 also informed that the exposure of officers of Commission of Railway Safety to new technologies and systems
 practiced abroad was not being done due to lack of funds for foreign travel.  The Commission also complained of lack
 of infrastructure and proper office machinery.  It was informed that the Commission did not have sufficient official
 vehicles, mobile phones and manpower for officials in comparison to officials of same status in Ministry of Railways. 
 The Committee was further informed that Railway had earlier agreed to provide mobile phones to the Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety and Commissioners of Railway Safety so that in an emergency they can be reached. 
 However, the commitment had not been honoured.  In the absence of such facilities, the Commissioners find it
 impossible to contact Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety and Railway Officials quickly for conveying
 information/seeking direction after the occurrence of an accident.
 
69.       The Committee notes with concern the constraints faced by the officers of the Commission of Railway Safety in
 performing their duties due to lack of budgetary allocations and proper infrastructure and office machinery.  The
 Committee feels that the Commission of Railway Safety need adequate budgetary support from the Government so that
 it does not have to look upon the Ministry of Railways for being able to effectively discharge its duties.  The
 Committee recommends that the budget allocation of Commission of Railway Safety should be substantially increased
 so that the Commission could take care of its essential requirements such as funds for foreign training, air travel within
 India, nominations to various training courses, membership to professional institutions etc. 
 
ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRIMA-FACIE CAUSE OF ACCIDENTS BY RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION
70.       The Committee observes that whenever a train accident occurs, the railway administration is quick to announce
 the prima-facie cause of the accident, even when the officials concerned are aware of the enormity of the accident and
 that, as provided in the Railway Act, Commissioner of Railway Safety would hold an enquiry to determine the exact
 cause of the accident.  However, if at a later date, the findings of the Commissioner of Railway Safety happen to
 coincide with the version earlier advanced by the railway officials, the Commission of Railway Safety is accused of a
 bias in favour of the Railways. Such actions affect the credibility of Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 
71.       The Committee is of the opinion that the unwritten convention that no one would give the cause of an accident,
 when an enquiry is pending, needs to be followed by the Railway administration.  The Committee recommends that the
 Railway administration should refrain from speculating and giving the prime-facie cause of an accident, which is
 required to be statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of Railway Safety.  This will ensure that the credibility of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is maintained and the Commissioners are not suspected of prejudice or bias in
 conducting their enquiries.
 
CONCLUSION
72.       The Committee is of the opinion that the Commission of Railway Safety is an important organisation of the
 Government and, in the prevailing circumstances, the Commission's hands need strengthening in all possible ways. The
 Committee recommends that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation incorporating the suggestion
 made by the Committee in this Report so that the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety could improve in
 the interest of the public travelling by Indian Railways.

 on absorption terms to the Commission.   The Committee is of the firm view that this would make the Commission
 independent, powerful and vigilant to the fullest extent.   This would definitely go a long way in dispelling the general
 impression that the Ministry of Railways unduly influences the Commission in its functioning as it is rightly said that
 justice should not only be done but it should also appear to have been done.

EFFECTIVENESS OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
 
The Committee is of the view that although the recommendations of the Commission of Railway Safety are not
 mandatory for the Ministry of Railways yet the situation brought out by the Commission of Railway Safety is highly
 unsatisfactory.  The Committee is of the view that the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway Safety
 should receive utmost importance from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee takes exception to the fact that, on
 certain occasions, the Ministry of Railways neither consults the Commission of Railway Safety before rejecting a
 recommendation nor furnishes reasons for not accepting the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway
 Safety.  The Committee strongly feels that the Commission of Railway Safety is a watch dog on behalf of the public at
 large.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Railways, should honour the commitment made by
 them to the Appointment Committee of Cabinet regarding consulting the Commission before rejecting a
 recommendation.   The Committee further recommends that it should be made mandatory for the Railway
 Administration not to reject or overrule any recommendations made by the Commissioners without a meeting between
 the Chairman, Railway Board and the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, where the matters can be discussed
 threadbare and agreements reached.  The Committee further recommends that while expressing their inability to accept
 the recommendations, the Railway Board should give detailed reasons for not accepting the recommendations.  The
 Committee also recommends that any decision taken by the Railway Board in consultation with the Commission of
 Railway Safety must not be revoked unilaterally by the Railway Board or Zonal Railway, without prior consultation
 and approval of the Commission.
(Para 27)
 
The Committee observes that a large number of new passenger trains are introduced every year to meet the demand of
 the traveling public.  While it does fulfil the requirements of the public, it has to be examined as to whether such an
 action is in the interest of safety and convenience of the traveling public.  The present system in the country is already
 overstressed and it is important to ensure that all infrastructure facilities cater to the safe running of additional trains
 with due safety margins.  It is essential that such facilities are in position before adding any burden of additional trains. 
 The introduction of additional trains involves the safety of the passengers.   The Committee is not convinced with the
 reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways with regard to not seeking the concurrence of Commission of Railway
 Safety before introduction of a new passenger train.  The Committee gives due weightage to the reply of the Ministry of
 Railways that before any new train is introduced, certification of available maintenance infrastructure at either end is
 given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and maintenance, after consulting all concerned
 agencies.  Ministry of Railway have also pointed out that concurrence of every new train does not fall under the legal
 duties of Commission of Railway Safety, as enumerated in the Railway Act, 1989.  The main task of the Commission is
 to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation/inspectional/audit and investigatory/advisory
 functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard to the soundness of rail
 construction and safety in train operation.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the sanction of Commission of
 Railway Safety must be necessary for Ministry of Railways before introducing any new passenger train.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be made mandatory for Ministry of Railways to seek the concurrence
