NILOTPAL BASU
Chairman
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing  Committee
 on Transport, Tourism & Culture.
 
Report
            India is one of the oldest civilizations in the world and its historical heritage and cultural glory has been the
 subject of interest of the entire humanity.  In a country like India, endowed with both tangible and intangible heritage of
 an immense cultural and artistic value, which also has a multi-religious cultural fabric, archaeology assumes a position
 of crucial importance.
2.         Keeping in view the importance of archaeology, the Archaeological Survey of India was established in the year
 1861 with the primary object of surveying and recording the archaeological monuments in India.  It has a long colonial
 history and its mandate has evolved at a very slow pace spread over centuries.  For the first time in the year 1880, an
 organized attempt was made to preserve the monuments from decay by appointing Mr. H.H. Cole as a curator of
 monuments, which also coincided, with the recognition of the fact that the preservation of the monument was the
 permanent responsibility of the State.  In 1899, the Archaeological Survey of India was administratively divided into
 five circles for the preservation, conservation, archaeological exploration and excavation on a permanent basis and with
 well defined polices.  With the advent of Lord Curzon as Viceroy, the Archaeological Survey of India was placed on a
 formal footing during the first decade of the 20
th century.  He appointed Mr. John Marshal as the Director General of
 Archaeological Survey of India, who undertook great excavation at Taxila, Sanchi, Sarnath etc. The concept of
 archaeological conservation of ancient monuments was added during the time of John Marshall.  Hundreds of
 monuments/sites were declared as protected monuments under the purview of the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act
 1904.  In 1944, Dr. R.E.M. Wheeler was appointed Director General of Archaeological Survey of India.  During his
 tenure he incorporated modern methods for carrying archaeological excavations and trained the staff of the Survey in
 excavations at Taxila, Arikamedu and Harappa.  Having indepth understanding and involvement he revolutionized the
 concept of archaeological excavation by introducing importance of stratigraphy.  Wheeler also started Horticulture
 Branch in Archaeological Survey of India to develop suitable gardens to create pollution free ambiance around
 monuments.  Thus, prior to independence a sound foundation was laid for the Archaeological Survey of India. 
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS IN THE POST INDEPENDENCE PERIOD:
3.         With the promulgation of the Constitution of India from 26
th January 1950, ‘archaeology’ has been made a
 Concurrent subject under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, which reads :
List I (Union List), item 67: ancient and historical monuments and records, and archaeological sites and remains
 declared by or under law by Parliament to be of national importance.
List II (State List), item 12: libraries, museums and other similar institutions controlled or financed by the State; ancient
 and historical monuments and records other than those declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national
 importance.
List III (Concurrent List), item 40: archaeological sites and remains other than those declared by or under law made by

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 Parliament to be of national importance.
4.         In fulfillment of the provisions of the Constitution, Parliament passed the “Ancient and Historical Monuments
 and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act” in 1951 by which all the monuments previously protected under the
 Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904 were re-declared to be of national importance.  In 1953, after the merger of
 the princely states with the rest of India, the Archaeological Survey of India took the additional responsibility of upkeep
 of the monuments in princely states.
5.         Currently, the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rules, 1959 and the
 Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 and Rules, 1973 are operational and empowers the Archaeological Survey of
 India in its functioning.  
PRESENT MANDATE OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
6.         The Archaeological Survey of India is the premier organization so far as the archaeological research, study,
 excavation of archaeological sites, conservation/preservation of centrally protected monuments, maintenance of site
 museums and overall regulation of antiquities and art objects are concerned. As an apex body in the field of
 archaeology, the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied which may be classified as
 under :-
Conservation and preservation of monuments/sites and remains;
Archaeological explorations and excavations;
Preservation of monuments and antiquarian remains;
Architectural survey of monuments;
Epigraphical and numismatic studies;
Setting up of the Site Museums;
Training in archaeology;
Archaeologial publications;
Archaeological expeditions abroad;
Implementation of Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972; and
Horticulture operation around ancient monuments and sites.
7.         Since the functions of Archaeological Survey of India are very broad and varied and India is endowed with
 tremendous historical and cultural heritage, the Committee decided to study the functioning of Archaeological Survey
 of India.  In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee decided to elicit the views of some independent
 experts in the field of archaeology.  Accordingly, the Committee heard the views of Shri S.S. Biswas, former Director
 General, National Museum and Shri Jagatpati Joshi, former Director General, Archaeological Survey of India on the
 17
th September and 1st October 2004 respectively.   On the basis of the information provided by these two independent
 experts and other documents provided to the Committee by the Ministry of Culture, the Committee took the oral
 evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture and the representatives of Archaeological Survey of India on the 29
th
 November and 27th December 2004 and the 20th June 2005 to get an indepth insight into the functioning of
 Archaeological Survey of India.
MONUMMENTS/SITES UNDER PROTECTION OF ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
8.         Archaeological Survey of India protects and maintains 3663 monuments/sites in total and also declared those
 monuments as of national importance.  All the monuments/sites protected by the Archaeological Survey of India are
 being conserved/preserved on need based requirement.  As regards classification of monuments into different
 categories, the ASI has drawn long term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites which are of historical,
 architectural and aesthetic value.  Classification of monuments is an ongoing process and depends upon the
 requirements and feasibility of management, protection of monuments/sites.  In view of the nature of importance,
 urgency for structural conservation, preservation and chemical preservation including environmental development and
 providing essential tourist facilities in all these monuments, the ASI has categorised the monuments as under: -
Category of Monuments
                             No. of Monuments
1. Group A                                                       18 (which are inscribed
on the World Heritage List of UNESCO and are ticketed)
2. Group B                                                      108  (These are other
ticketed monuments/sites)    
3. Group C                   3537 (Unticketed
monuments/sites)
However, the Ministry made it clear that the above categorization is not a formal one, but for the convenience sake the

91stReport of Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/91streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:19]
 monuments have been categorized. 
9.         The Committee notes that the ASI has drawn long-term programme to protect all 3663 monuments/sites of
 national importance out of which 3537 monuments/sites are unticketed.  These monuments have also been classified
 into three categories viz. Group A, B and C for convenience.    The Committee is however aware that there are many
 sites/monuments under the protection/maintenance of Archaeological Survey of India which are located in interior
 areas of various States but are lying unattended. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Culture should
 equally treat the revenue earning and not-earning sites and efforts should be made for integrated infrastructure
 development and conservation/preservation of all monuments/sites with encompassing facilities for tourists, so as to
 give a major fillip to cultural tourism in the country as well as attracting overseas visitors.                   
ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
10.       At present the Archaeological Survey of India is functioning as an attached office under the Ministry of Culture,
 which is headed by the Union Minister for Culture.  The Ministry of Culture has a Secretary level officer, who looks
 after various attached and subordinate office in the Ministry.  Being an attached office, the Archaeological Survey of
 India has its own head designated as Director General.  The Director General, in turn, is assisted by an Additional
 Director General, a Joint Director General and a group of Directors.  At present there are 10 Directors assisting the
 Director General in performing duties.  For administrative convenience and research purposes, the Archaeological
 Survey of India  is divided into 21 Circles headed by a Superintending Archaeologist, who is further assisted by Deputy
 Superintending Archaeologist., Deputy S.A.E., A.S.A., A.S.A.E., Ass & C.As.  There are 6 Excavation Branches, on
 Prehistory Branch, one Building Survey Project, two Temple Survey Projects, two Epigraphy Branches and one
 Science Branch functioning in the Archaeological Survey of India on different field and research project.
11.       The Archaeological Survey of India is headed by a Director General.  Some of the important functions and
 responsibilities of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India are as under:
To function as the head of the Archaeological Survey of India which is primarily engaged on (a) basic research in
 various disciplines of archaeology, including (i)archaeological excavations and explorations (ii) protection of
 monuments/sites of national importance, their proper maintenance and upkeep and carrying of archaeological
 conservation as well as chemical preservation of these monuments/sites; prevention of vandalism/encroachment at
 these monuments/sites, setting up and maintenance of site, museums, environmental development of monuments/sites;
 (iii) bringing out of archaeological publications (iv) epigraphical research (v) operation of antiquarian law viz. Ancient
 Monuments and Archaeological sites and Remains Act-1958 and Rules 1959; as well as Antiquities & Art Treasures
 Act, 1972 and Rules 1976; (vi) bringing out of archaeological publications (vii) maintenance and upkeep of
 archaeological libraries.
Laying down of archaeological policy in the country, and to issue licences for conducting archaeological excavations by
 various states/research Institution and generally guide archaeological activities in the country.
12.       The Committee noted that the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India was being filled up by
 the Government from Indian Administrative Service (IAS) for a fairly long period.  During its interaction with one
 independent expert on the functioning of Archaeological Survey of India, the Committee was informed that the
 Government had issued a notification in May 2002, according to which  the Director General, Archaeological Survey of
 India should have a Master’s Degree in Indian History/Archaeology/allied subjects and should have eighteen years of
 administrative experience with, at least, five years in the field of archaeology. The Committee noted that the
 notification had not been implemented, and since the last 12 years, the Director General deputed to the Archaeological
 Survey of India had no basic qualification or knowledge in archaeology.
13.       The same independent expert while submitting his views before the Committee on the functioning of
 Archaeological Survey of India also emphasized that the practice of filling up the post of Director General,
 Archaeological Survey of India from Indian Administrative Service on deputation basis had adversely affected the
 functioning of Archaeological Survey of India and stated as under:
“This is relating to the appointment of all the scientific officers, specially the head of the department i.e. the Director
 General who has been coming on deputation basis from the Ministry.  This aspect is very much related to the
 functioning of the ASI.  If the bureaucrats who have little knowledge of it, are manning the scientific department or

SARASVATI PROJECT
25.       The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, govern excavations in India.  The
 Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India grants licenses to various excavation agencies, both government
 and autonomous, for conducting excavations on the recommendations of the standing Committee of the Central
 Advisory Board of Archaeology (CABA).  The criteria for selecting a site for excavation are as under:
bridging of missing gaps(s) in the cultural sequence of Indian archaeology,
throwing more light on lesser known cultures.
Salvage archaeology in the event of a site being submerged by a dam or being destroyed or damaged due to absolutely
 necessary development works, natural calamities.

th

 findings of the Steering Committee that out of 56 excavations, 17 belong to the category of large-scale excavation and

 1969 could be published in 2003, entitled “Kalibangan – the Early Harappans” as memoirs of Archaeological Survey

 still ongoing and some of them are at various stages of completion.

 information on excavated structures, stratigraphical features, supported by maps, illustrations – photo-documentation
 and line-drawings of excavated structures, potteries, artifacts, and other materials.  The report also would have to
 incorporate detailed technical and scientific reports and bibliographical references.  Since a huge body of data is
 generated in course of excavation, it takes time to organize and describe that exhaustive database on factual and
 interpretative lines.  For report writing, a team of excavators, who participated in that very excavation, is required to
 discuss, prepare research notes, and correlate the excavation findings for description in terms of time and space.  This is
 true in case of all excavations.  This has been further complicated the officers were sometime transferred before they
 could complete the reports.

 published in the Indian Archaeology – A review (IAR), an annual publication of the Archaeological Survey of India.

 whether there were any safeguards in the transfer policy to ensure that transfer of the officials did not affect the ongoing
 work assigned to them, especially in preparation of excavation reports.  In reply, the Archaeological Survey of India
 informed the Committee that there exists no specific transfer policy for the staff in the ASI.  However, according to the
 prevalent practice, efforts are being made to adjust the staff on promotion up to non-gazetted level in the same
 Circles/Branches subject to the availability of vacancies in the respective grades, failing which they are transferred to
 the next nearest Circle/branch.  Requests from the officers and staff for transfer from one Circle to another are
 considered on the basis of merit keeping in view the facts and circumstances explained by them in their applications.  In
 order to ensure the timely completion of the ongoing excavation works and their reports, it has been decided in
 principle to allow the concerned officers to complete the ongoing excavations and their detailed reports before they are
 transferred to other places.
46.       The Committee is of the view that if excavation reports are not written, then all the taxpayers’ money spent on
 them goes waste.  Also, in absence of timely publication of excavation reports, the achievements of Archaeological
 Survey of India largely remain unnoticed by the public.  The Committee is extremely dissatisfied to observe that
 despite its repeated recommendations, the position in respect of writing of excavation reports has not improved much. 
 However, the Committee is hopeful that the steps now initiated by Archaeological Survey of India for clearing the
 backlog in respect of writing excavation reports would yield some positive results.  The Committee recommends that
 the Archaeological Survey of India should enforce a fixed time frame for writing excavation reports after the
 excavation work has been completed, so that the public at large is not deprived of the vital right to information.  The
 Committee also recommends that the ASI should ensure that officials engaged in a particular excavation work are not
 transferred till such time that they complete the excavations and submit their reports.

CONSERVATION/PRESERVATION OF MONUMENTS AND REGISTRATION OF ANTIQUITIES
54.       The Committee also enquired about the procedure adopted for conservation/preservation of the monuments.  The
 Committee was informed that whenever an ancient structure or an archaeological site/remain is considered be of
 national importance, a proposal to this effect is initiated by the circle office and sent to the Director General,
 Archaeological Survey of India along with its historical, archaeological and architectural importance.  On receipt of the
 approval of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, the proposal is forwarded to the State Government
 with detailed drawings for the counter signature of the Deputy Commissioner/Commissioner concerned.  On receipt of
 the revenue data duly counter signed, the Central Government issues a notification of its intentions to declare the
 monument as of national importance with a two months notice.  On the expiry of notice period and after considering the
 objections, if any, a final Gazette notification is issued for declaring the said monument as a monument of national
 importance.
55.       The State Governments are consulted if the proposed monument is State protected and is proposed to be taken
 over by the Archaeological Survey of India.  In all other cases, State Governments are involved only to the extent of
 preparation of relevant revenue papers required for the notification or subsequently, if land or building compensation is
 involved.
56.       The Committee was further informed that the basic guidelines for conservation have been framed with an
 objective to prolong the life of monuments without the loss of artistic and historical values.  It is important for
 archaeological values to preserve the original fabric of the monument to the extent possible.  Archaeological Survey of
 India follows a Conservation Manual which contains detailed guidelines for execution of conservation works.  The
 conservation and preservation of monuments aim at :
its preservation without disfigurement or alteration of its character;
its maintenance in a proper and attractive condition;
the complete examination of its remains and documentary evidence concerning it; and
 
the preparation of monographs, guide books and reports so that its historical and artistic interest may be perpetuated.
57.       Apart from this the monuments which had garden around them as part of their original design are taken up for
 restoration and maintenance and wherever it was not part of original layout/feature, beautification through landscaping
 is also undertaken.  However, it has been decided to compile a comprehensive conservation manual during the 10
th Five
 Year Plan period incorporating extant guidelines of Archaeological Survey of India and relevant features of
 internationally acceptable conservation guidelines and norms.
58.       The Committee is of the view that beautification and development of archaeological sites no doubt adds to the
 ambience of these sites.  However, the Committee recommends that while taking up work, the focus should be on

 merging it together afterwards.  The explanation put forth by the Ministry was as follows:-
“Initially it was proposed to set up two separate Missions – National Mission on Built Heritage, Monuments and Sites
 and National Mission on Antiquities.  The estimated cost for the two Missions when the proposals were initially
 formulated was Rs.250 crore and Rs.150 crore respectively.  Based on the comments received from the Planning
 Commission, Department of Expenditure, IFD etc., the matter was reconsidered in consultation with the Archaeological
 Survey of India.  It was suggested that since the nature of work for the two Missions was complementary to each other
 both the Missions should be carried out by one structural network since in both the cases, the nodal agency was going
 to be Archaeological Survey of India.  The overall project cost of Rs.400 crore also needed to be pruned drastically
 since no provision had been made in the 10
th Five Year Plan for these Missions.  While merging and recasting the two
 Missions it was therefore decided to reduce the Missions’ outlay to about Rs.90 crore to make it compact and viable so
 that there is no time overrun beyond the five years period prescribed for the Project.  The Mission would be able to
 generate public awareness and synergy between Archaeological Survey of India and several other institutions working
 in the field.  The two Missions proposals on Built Heritage and Antiquities have been merged.  Initially two documents
 for two Missions i.e. Antiquities and Built heritage were prepared with Archaeological Survey of India as the Nodal
 Agency.  As the objectives of both the Missions were overlapping and Mission structure had been streamlined, it was
 felt that a single Mission structure for both the Missions i.e. for Built Heritage and Antiquities could undertake the
 work.  Moreover the expertise required for undertaking the work of both the Missions is similar; hence twin Mission
 proposal has been recast into a single Mission proposal.  By merging them together, the financial outlay required for
 undertaking both the Missions has been greatly reduced and the goals are also justified.”

ORGANISATIONAL SET UP AND THE POST OF DIRECTOR GENERAL OF THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL
 SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee is not in agreement with the argument put- forth by the Ministry of Culture that the appointment of
 generalist administrator as Director General will not hamper the development of Archaeological Survey of India as a
 scientific organisation.  The Committee is shocked to note that even after the Gazette Notification of May 2002, the
 Government has not been able to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the
 requirements of the notification and has been merely filling up the post from Indian Administrative Service on
 deputation basis.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the Government preferred to fill up the highest post of
 an apex institution requiring very high standards of technical qualification with a generalist administrator.  The
 Committee is of the view that a person who has no basic qualification or knowledge of archaeology cannot handle the
 apex responsibility of a Scientific Institution like Archaeological Survey of India.  Unless the leader of the
 Archaeological Survey of India is having the professional expertise, it is very difficult to give a lead.  This has also
 dampened the spirits of the senior officers in the feeder grade of the organization who may never get the opportunities
 to serve as senior most officer of their parent organization.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
 taken to fill up the post of Director General, Archaeological Survey of India as per the requirements of the Notification
 of May 2002, at the earliest.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA AS A SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL DEPARTMENT
The Committee is constrained to note that even after a lapse of fifteen years from the date of issue of the notification in
 this regard no concrete action was taken by Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India for developing
 Archaeological Survey of India as a Scientific and Technical Department, which amply indicates the administrative
 apathy towards the whole issue.  The Committee regrets that no internal exercise was undertaken by Ministry of
 Culture and Archaeological Survey of India during the last fifteen years for availing the benefits and privileges which
 could be extended to the Archaeological Survey of India as a Science and Technology department.  The Committee
 observes that there has been deviation in the working of Archaeological Survey of India and that it has failed in terms
 of developing Archaeological Survey of India not merely as an administrative body but also as a spearhead for
 consolidating the scientific discipline of archaeology in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the
 Archaeological Survey of India needs to reinvent itself, not merely as an administrative wing of the Government, but as
 an agency for protecting and safeguarding our national heritage, which involves a lot of scientific and technical work. 
 Unless the Archaeological Survey of India converts itself fully into a scientific and technical organization, the basic
 role and function of the organisation will be defeated.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture and
 Archaeological Survey of India should, without any further loss of time, take necessary follow-up action on the
 recommendations of the Committee chaired by Director General, Archaeological Survey of India so as to avail the
 benefits which accrue to a Science and Technology department.  The Committee also recommends that, if required, the
 Ministry of Culture should also take necessary legislative action to make Archaeological Survey of India Science and
 Technology department in the true sense.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the observations/ recommendations as
 contained in its Eighty-fourth Report on Demands for Grants (2005-2006) (Demand No. 86) of Department of Road
 Transport and Highways, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 29
th April, 2005.

nd September, 2005 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been categorised as follows: -

3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as

4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of Action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Department.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Eighty-fourth
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government, and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
ANALYSIS OF THE TENTH PLAN PROVISIONS AND ANNUAL                                    PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 20) 
 
5.         The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalization of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of
 Road Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are
 inadequate while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.  
 The Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned
 are delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature
 and are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE
 stage.  The Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways.  The lack of a proper monitoring system in the Department is exemplified by the delay and non-completion
 of the construction of flyover at Murthal in Haryana and the failure of the Department of Road Transport and Highways
 in verifying the credentials of the contractors who had submitted forged bank guarantees.  The Committee observes that
 the budget allocations of the Department of Road Transport and Highways have been substantially increased during
 2005-06. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should devise
 strategies, whereby they are able to fully utilize the funds at their disposal.  They should also evolve some mechanism
 to identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such hindrances in coordination with all the
 concerned agencies.  This would also help them to avoid time overrun and consequential cost overrun of the projects to
 be executed by them.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT:
 
6.         The main reason for non-utilization of the approved funds of 2004-05 was non-execution of loan agreements
 with Asian Development Bank (ADB) and World Bank for Projects under NHDP-Phase-II due to procedural delay like
 clearance from ADB / World Bank, high tender rates, delay in signing loan agreement, etc.  However, most of the
 problems have now been resolved. 
 
7.         Out of total length of 6736 kms under NHDP Phase-II, projects consisting of 814 km. are already under
 implementation and the projects for the length of 5722 kms are scheduled for award by Dec., 2005 in phased manner. 
 The projects for the balance 200 kms. shall be awarded in the next financial year 2006-07.  With the award of these
 projects, substantial expenditure is expected to be incurred on their implementation. 
 
8.         Major initiatives and steps to remove constraints and bottlenecks in the implementation of North-South and East-
West Corridor have been undertaken to expedite the implementation of projects and making improvement in the internal

9.         The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
(Recommendation at Para 29) 
 
10.       The Committee notes that the target date of completion of the Golden Quadrilateral has been revised twice i.e.
 from December 2003 to December 2004 and now up to December 2005.  The Committee had discussed this issue in its

nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and recommended that
 the Government should take all necessary steps to make sure that the works proposed to be completed by December
 2004 are completed within that period.  However, the Committee notes that the progress of four-laning on the Golden
 Quadrilateral project as on December 2004 was only 74%.  Thus, the steps taken by Department of Road Transport and
 Highways for timely completion of the project had not been adequate.  The Committee, therefore, would like to

ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2005-06
(Recommendation at Para No. 10&11)
 
5.The Committee expresses its concern over the failure of Department of Shipping to spend the approved outlay. 
 During the year 2004-05, out of the budgeted amount of Rs.2419.66 crore the Department could spent only Rs.1400.99
 crore which clearly indicates the poor fiscal management in the Department of Shipping.  The Committee observes that
 even while revising allocations, little consideration has been paid to the actual expenditure incurred in the past.  This
 shows that budgetary and revised estimates have always been made without taking into account the actual requirements
 as experienced in the previous years.
 6.The Committee feels that Department of Shipping has not evolved effective system or planning to systematically
 anticipate, assess and project its actual requirements of funds otherwise the investments could have yielded
 commensurate returns.  The Committee recommends that in future, the Department of Shipping should be transparent
 and realistic while making projections of required funds so that resources may not remain unused and are allocated
 more judiciously.

7.         The Annual Plan outlay during the year 2004-05 for the Port Sector was Rs.1066.95 crores. Actual expenditure
 was Rs.341.62 crores (Provisional).

 of Major Ports and heads of other organizations. Allocations for various projects under the Annual Plan are made after
 carrying out an assessment of the requirements on year to year basis. The Annual Plan proposals are formulated about
 five to six months in advance before the commencement of the Annual Plan period after factoring in the anticipated
 expenditure during the current year and the assessed requirements in the ensuing Annual Plan year for on-going
 projects and taking into account the assessed requirement of funds for the new projects to be taken up during the
 ensuing Annual Plan year. Requirements of funds at the Revised Estimates stage is projected after carrying out a review
 of the progress in the expenditure during the year till that time and after taking into account the anticipated expenditure
 during the remaining part of the year. This does not necessarily follow a uniform or standard pattern every year.

 generally mismatch between the allocations and the actual expenditure. The ports were advised that there should be
 realistic approach while proposing the Annual Plan outlay for 2005-06 and that only token provision may be kept for

 of the Committee will be kept in view while finalizing the allocation for Annual Plans in future also.

SETHUSAMUDRAM SHIP CHANNEL PROJECT
(Recommendation at Para 36)
 26.      The Committee notes the Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project is of great economic and strategic importance
 which will connect the Gulf of Mannar to Bay of Bengal so that the ship moving between East and West coast of India
 could have a continuous navigable sea route within their own territorial waters and the proposed channel save upto 424
 nautical miles of travel and about 30 hours of sailing time for ships.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that
 Ministry of Environment & Forests has also given environmental clearance to the project and a special purpose vehicle
 has been incorporated to raise finance to create and operate navigable channel.  The Committee expects that the project
 once completed will serve the strategic and national security interests besides spuring the overall economic
 development of coastal districts of southern states.  The Committee however, recommends that while taking up the
 implementation of the project, the Department of Shipping must give due attention to the likely effect of natural
 calamities particularly one like as Tsunami which hit southern states during December 2004 and safety measures may
 be incorporated accordingly.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
27.       The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are accepted.The Government sanction for implementing
 Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project at a cost of Rs.2427.40 crores has been issued on 1
st June, 2005. The animation
 models of the Tsunami of 26th December, 2004 available with the Tuticorin Port Trust indicates that the project area
 was the least affected on the east coast by the Tsunami. Hydrodynamic modeling studies recently carried out have
 confirmed the earlier findings that increase in magnitude of the current in the post-channel era will be only along the
 channel in Adam’s Bridge with no change in current status alongside the channel. The issues relating to Tsunami and
 impact of cyclonic storms over the channel were also duly examined by the Ministry of Environment & Forests before
 according environmental clearance. However, during the execution phase, suggestions of the experts will be duly taken
 into consideration by the project authorities to ensure that the impact of natural calamities on the channel is
 insignificant. An Environmental Monitoring Committee comprising experts/officials has been set up by the
 Government for monitoring of various environmental issues connected with the implementation of the project which
 will meet at least once a month and submit its report to the Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport & Highways.

SHORTAGE OF ACCOMMODATION  IN THE STAR AND BUDGET HOTELS
(Recommendation at Para Nos. 79 & 80)
65.       The Committee notes with serious concern that there is a shortfall in hotel accommodation in all star categories particularly in the budget hotel segment though India is the second fastest growing country in the
travel and Tourism sector and is growing at the rate of 8.8% annually.  India has witnessed a tremendous growth in tourism sector registering a positive growth of about 30.2% in domestic tourism and increase of 23.5% in
terms of foreign tourist arrivals.  The Committee feels that poor tourism infrastructure may hinder the growth of tourism.  The Committee observes that the accommodation shortage is due to scarcity of prime location and
rigid land use norms.  The Committee recommends the ministry to take coordinated efforts with all the State/Union Territories for allotment of plots at prime locations and provide incentives for meeting the demand. 
Priority should also be given to meet increasing demand for capacity addition and uplifting tourism infrastructure to support the growth of tourism in the country.
66.       The Committee is also of the view that Infrastructure is the key to the development of any economy and to boost economic growth in the country.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that a full-fledged
infrastructure status should be given to tourism and hospitality sector for the growth of tourism in a big way.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
67.       A Task Force under the Chairmanship of the Additional Director General(Tourism), to look into the modalities for development of tourist infrastructure including accommodation in the star categories and budget
hotels in the country has recently been set up in the Ministry of Tourism.  The first meeting of the Task Force was held on 11
th
 May, 2005. The State Governments have been requested to adopt a proactive land use policy
to make available sites for hotel industry and to have a liberal approach towards Floor Area Rates(FAR) and Floor Space Index(FSI) etc.  The matter regarding grant of a full-fledged status of infrastructure was taken up at

the level of Secretary(Tourism) with the Ministry of Finance  letters dated 23.11.2004 and 20.1.2005.  Ministry of Finance has again been requested to expedite the matter.

little attention to the Information Technology initiatives and has not achieved much progress in this field, which is very crucial for providing vital information to the tourist at the shortest time span.  However, the
Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism is planning to introduce a toll free Telecom based facilitation service for the benefit of tourists and the existing official website on tourism has also been revamped to provide
reliable and detailed information on India and Indian tourism products.  The Committee hopes that this facility will be made available to the tourists within the stipulated period of six months.  The Committee feels that the
concentration has to be focussed on certain areas especially at grass root level and recommends that there should be a centralized system for dissemination of all essential information through the web database so as to
establish a vital linkage with the people at large and the website should also be linked with all the State websites.  The Committee notes that the present official website on tourism has a lot of information but these are

ASSESSMENT OF ANNUAL PLAN 2004-05 AND ALLOCATION FOR    2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 9)
5.         The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the outlay approved during 2004-05. 
 The Ministry anticipated to utilize an amount of Rs.1473.03 crore out of the approved allocation of Rs.1620.98 crore during
 the year 2004-05, which exemplifies the poor financial management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Committee feels
 that there is a lack of proper planning in the various organizations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a result of which the
 Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the concerned agencies to make a realistic assessment of their financial
 requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.         The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  Due care would be taken to ensure that Plan
 budgets are formulated on realistic basis so as to ensure that the same are properly utilized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7.         The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should formulate Plan budgets on realistic basis and also review the
 same at quarterly intervals to monitor the utilization of the allocations under different Budget Heads.  The Committee
 therefore recommends that the exercise undertaken during the preparation of Revised Budget Estimates should involve a
 detailed review of the progress of various projects rather than conducting the same in a routine manner.
INDIAN AIRLINES
(Recommendation at Para 22)
8.         The Committee would like to record its appreciation regarding the role played by Indian Airlines and Alliance Air in
 evacuation of people from Andaman & Nicobar Islands after the tsunami disaster and heavy snowfall in parts of Jammu &
 Kashmir in the winter season this year.    The Committee notes that Indian Airlines is expected to earn a profit of Rs.8.75
 crores by the end of the financial year 2004-05.   The Committee understands the reasons for the low amount of profit likely
 to be earned by Indian Airlines.   The Committee observes that Indian Airlines does not have sufficient number of aircraft to
 optimally utilize the domestic seat capacity available in the country and the average age of the aircraft available with Indian
 Airlines is on the higher side.   Also Indian Airlines has to take the lion's share in undertaking social responsibilities of the
 nation.   As part of its social obligation, Indian Airlines also has to fly to those unremunerative destinations, which other
 airlines choose not to fly due to commercial considerations.   The Committee, therefore, appreciates that, inspite of the odds
 being placed heavily against the company, Indian Airlines would be ending the financial year 2004-05 with marginal profits.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
9.         Ministry of Civil Aviation would like to thank the Committee for its views with regard to role and financial
 performance of Indian Airlines/Alliance Air.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
            10.       The Committee desires that Indian Airlines/Alliance Air would maintain their special role in fulfilling the
 social obligations of the nation especially during the times of extreme distress.
(Recommendation at Para 26)
11.       The Committee notes that the revision of scales of pay of employees of Indian Airlines had become due on 1.1.1997.  
 However, even after a lapse of a period of more than eight years, the Government is yet to take a decision in the matter.  
 The Committee feels that the revision of scales of pay would contribute towards preventing the exodus of trained manpower
 from Indian Airlines.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take an early decision in the
 matter so that the employees of Indian Airlines are not deprived of their legitimate right to the revision of scales of pay
 which has been pending for long.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
12.       The Government has noted the recommendation.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13.       The Committee expresses its anguish over the evasive comments of the Ministry offered in response to the

OPENING OF INTERNATIONAL ROUTES FOR PRIVATE AIRLINES
(Recommendation at Para 32)
17.       The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding its decision to open
 up international skies to a particular airlines and granting it passage rights to some international routes on the opening day of
 its public offer. The Committee is of the view that the timing of the decision pushed up the company’s IPO prospects and the
 policy adopted by the Government and the clearances granted by the Ministry to the company were too close to the public
 offer of the company to be termed as coincidence.  The Committee feels that grant of speedy clearances to the company
 helped the airline get a good opening for its equity offering.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the conduct of
 Ministry of Civil Aviation in granting speedy clearances to the airline and the policy changes should be further enquired into
 by an independent agency.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
18.       Minister (Civil Aviation) has clarified the position of the Government in a statement made in the Rajya Sabha on
 13.05.2005.  It is reiterated that the decision to permit Indian scheduled airlines to operate to foreign destinations was the
 culmination of a long process and was consciously taken after due consideration.
 19.      Requests for allowing private airlines to operate on international routes were received in the Ministry for the past
 several years from various quarters like industry associations and trade bodies as well as Ministries like Tourism. It was
 emphasised that this would help in better utilisation of India’s bilateral rights, improve connectivity and create business
 opportunities within the country, which in turn would help the national economy as a whole.
 
20.       In fact, the process to allow Indian scheduled carriers to fly abroad began as early as October, 2003 with the
 announcement of the Prime Minister during the visit of Sri Lankan Prime Minister to permit private airlines of India to fly to
 Sri Lanka.  In December 2003, the Government decided to also allow private airlines to operate to all SAARC countries. In
 pursuance of these decisions, two private airlines - Jet Airways and Air Sahara - commenced operations to Sri Lanka and
 Nepal. It is, therefore, pertinent to mention that the policy to allow private carriers to operate abroad is not a recent one. 
21.       The Naresh Chandra Committee, constituted to prepare a road map for the civil aviation sector in their report
 submitted in December 2003, also recommended that private airlines be allowed to operate on international routes in view of
 the under utilisation of capacity in the international segment, particularly during peak season. The Committee also noted that
 India was using barely 40% of its bilateral rights.
22.       In the Cabinet Meeting held on 10.12.2003, while allowing private airlines to operate to SAARC countries, the
 Cabinet also directed Ministry of Civil Aviation to bring up a comprehensive note on liberalising international air services. 
 In pursuance of this decision, a proposal was initiated for allowing private airlines to operate on international routes except

 Gulf countries. This proposal was considered by the previous Government in the Cabinet Meeting held on 4.2.2004.  
 However, a decision on this proposal was postponed.
23.       After the present Government assumed office, the Cabinet in its meeting on 8 th September, 2004, while approving
 this Ministry’s proposal to sign the Air Services Agreement with Tunisia, directed the Ministry to bring up a proposal for
 building up of capacity both in public and private sector for operation of air services for optimum utilisation of our bilateral
 rights.
24.       Accordingly, a proposal to allow private airlines to operate on international sectors except the Gulf countries was
 inter alia placed before the Cabinet after following all established procedures. The draft Cabinet note was circulated to all
 concerned Ministries on 10.11.2004 and after receipt of their comments, the proposal was sent to Cabinet Secretariat in
 December 2004. Thereafter, the Cabinet considered and approved the proposal in its meeting on 29.12.2004.  Thus, it may
 be observed that the proposal was moved in accordance with Cabinet’s directions and the necessary procedures were fully
 adhered to. 
25.       It may also be mentioned that the contention that rights were allocated to a particular airline on the opening day of its
 public offer does not appear to be factually correct. In pursuance of Government’s decision taken on 29.12.2004, the first
 traffic rights were allocated to Air India and other Indian scheduled carriers for operations to UK on 31.01.2005, as the
 airlines were required to confirm their entitlements to the UK authorities for slot allocation at UK airports. However, this
 date has no relevance to the IPO offer of a private airline, as the opening day of the IPO issue of a particular airline was
 apparently on 18.02.2005. In any case, Government’s decisions were in no way guided by the dates of issue of IPO’s of
 private companies. 
26.       It is, therefore, evident that the decision to allow Indian scheduled carriers to operate on international routes was the
 culmination of a well considered process over a period of one year, starting in December 2003. The sequence of events
 clearly reveals that the Government decision had nothing to do with the IPO issue of any airline. It was entirely based on the
 need to allow Indian carriers to optimise our entitlements vis-à-vis foreign airlines. In view of the facts enumerated, no
 enquiry into this issue by an independent agency is warranted, since this Ministry has been fully transparent in its processes,
 has adhered to all procedures and no issue emerges that needs to be investigated.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27.       The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry which consists of the details of the process of decision
 making in the matter of allowing Indian scheduled carriers/private airlines to operate on international routes except the Gulf
 countries.  However, the Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry has given evasive reply to the main issue in
 question regarding the grant of speedy clearances to a particular airline in pursuance of above decision.  The Committee
 feels that if the Ministry is confident about the legality and transparency of the matter, as it has been attempted to be made
 out in the reply, there should be no objection against an inquiry by an independent agency.  The Committee, therefore,
 reiterates its recommendation that the matter of grant of speedy clearances to the particular airlines to enhance its IPO
 prospects, after the decision of the Government to allow Indian scheduled Carriers to operate on international routes, should
 be inquired into by an independent agency. 
(Recommendation at Para 35)
28.       The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by Ministry of Civil Aviation with regard to the criteria
 adopted in selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to fly on international routes.  The Committee feels that
 there is an element of arbitrariness in imposing restrictions on airlines in terms of experience of flying etc. and not allowing
 all the domestic scheduled airlines to fly on international routes.  By imposing such restrictions, the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation did not give a fair chance to the other scheduled domestic private airline operating in the country.  The Committee
 is also of the view that Ministry of Civil Aviation did not carry out any due diligence of the performance record of the
 existing private sector airlines in terms of fulfilling the social obligations by flying to remote and inaccessible areas of the
 country and utilizing the costly technologies installed at the airports such a ILS CAT-III system.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
29.       Minister (Civil Aviation) has clarified the position of the Government in a statement made in the Rajya Sabha on
 13.05.2005.  The minimum requirement prescribed for airlines to qualify for operations on international routes is entirely
 based on the consideration that only airlines with proven track records in the domestic sectors should be allowed to operate
 internationally. This is particularly important, as the Government does not want airlines to withdraw or curtail operations on
 domestic routes once they start international operations. Therefore, a minimum fleet strength of 20 aircraft has been
 prescribed. This would ensure sustained domestic connectivity while enabling the airlines to gain greater experience and put
 in place the required infrastructure facilities for operation on international routes at a later stage. 
30.       The eligibility criteria of five years’ operation in the domestic sector is also a carefully thought-out decision based on
 advice received from the safety regulator, Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). Experience of five years’ operations
 in domestic sector was considered necessary as a start up airline invariably needs that much time to put its entire
 maintenance and other safety related systems in place. It may be appreciated that once airlines start operating to foreign
 countries, they would be subject to safety checks by regulatory authorities of other countries. It is, therefore, essential that

31.       It may also be mentioned that on the date of Government decision in this regard, i.e. 29.12.2004, there were only

 per the eligibility criteria decided. One airline, which did not qualify, was in any case only about one year old and had also

32.       As regards due diligence and performance records of airlines, once an airline has operated in domestic sectors for 5
 years in accordance with the laid down standards, its track record in safety and overall performance would have been
 adequately monitored by DGCA. There are stringent safety requirements that the airlines are required to follow while
 operating on domestic sector and each of the airlines is also required to meet social obligations by adhering to route
 dispersal guidelines.  There is strict monitoring of their adherence to the route dispersal guidelines on a monthly basis by the
 DGCA.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
33.       The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that there are only two minimum eligibility criteria prescribed
 for selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to operate on international routes, namely, a minimum fleet
 strength of 20 aircrafts and a minimum experience of five years operations on domestic routes.  The Committee also notes
 that the basic policy of the Government to allow the scheduled carriers to operate on international routes has been framed
 after due consideration of the Report of Naresh Chandra Committee, which was submitted to the Ministry in December
 2003.  The said committee had reportedly revealed that we are presently using only 40% of our bilateral rights.  However,
 the Committee feels that the steep restrictions imposed by the Ministry are impediments in achieving the basic objectives
 behind the new policy to mitigate under capacity in the international segment and to enhance global connectivity to and
 from different states in the country.   The Committee recommends that in view of the irreversible nature of the new policy,
 the Ministry should review its prescribed standards regarding fleet strength, maintenance facilities, safety systems etc. for
 granting licences to new airlines in the domestic sector, taking into consideration the requirements for the international
 sector also.  Such a review would enable the relaxation of the existing stringent restrictions on Indian scheduled airlines for
 international operations. The Committee also notes that the stringent restrictions have not been able to avoid the denial of
 flights to one of the private airlines to destinations in the United States of America.
(Recommendation at Para 39)
34.       The Committee notes that there is a contradiction between the objectives stated by the Ministry of Civil Aviation in
 allowing private airlines to fly to international destinations and the routes actually allotted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 to the private airlines.  The Committee observes that the basic objective of the Government in allowing private airlines to fly
 to international destinations was providing connectivity to such destination which the Ministry has not been able to provide
 in the past because of lack of capacity of Air India and Indian Airlines.  However, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has granted
 permission to these private airlines to fly to those destinations, which were already being serviced, by Air India and Indian
 Airlines.  Hence the stated position of the Government in this respect is in total contradiction with the actual decisions of the
 Government and the basic objective of the Government to provide connectivity to new international destinations has been
 defeated.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
35.       While it is the intention of the Ministry to encourage operation of eligible airlines to newer destinations, it may be
 emphasised that the primary objective behind the decision to permit Indian scheduled carriers to fly abroad is to ensure
 optimal utilisation of traffic rights available to India. The traffic rights available to India through various bilateral
 agreements were under-utilised for a variety of reasons.
36.       India offers tremendous opportunities to airlines because of the rapidly growing international traffic to/from this
 country.  This potential was largely exploited by foreign airlines. While it is true that most of the routes so far allocated to
 Indian scheduled airlines are also being served by Air India/Indian Airlines, this would ensure better utilisation of the traffic
 rights available with us. Otherwise, the traffic on these routes would have been diverted to foreign airlines allowing them to
 derive disproportionate benefits.  It would not be desirable if foreign airlines  were allowed to carry traffic to/from India in
 increasing numbers while restricting our own airlines – public or private – from operating on international routes. 
37.       It may also be mentioned that most of the routes allocated to foreign airlines have witnessed significant growth of
 traffic in recent past and therefore provide ample commercial opportunities to all airlines.  It is also the considered view of
 the Ministry that direct connectivity between point-to-point destinations needs to be encouraged.  For instance, if the traffic
 size between UK and India is significant, the commercial opportunities out of this demand should ideally be utilised by
 Indian carriers or carriers of UK. The Government have approached the issue of liberalization of international air services
 with these objectives in mind. 
38.       It may also be emphasised that implementation of the policy is still at an early stage. As the process evolves,
 Government will continue to take stock of the situation and it is inevitable that newer destinations will get added over a
 period of time.

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
39.       The Committee is not satisfied with the reply.  The Ministry has not charted out any long-term plan for the
 implementation of the new policy of opening up the international skies to the Indian scheduled airlines.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry should frame a comprehensive plan identifying international sectors to be covered by Air
 India/Indian Airlines/International Scheduled Carriers so as to avoid any conflict of interests and at the same time ensuring
 full realization of the objective to enhance utilization of traffic rights available to India.  
 
REVIEW OF ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
(Recommendation at Para 42)
 40.      The Committee is of the view that the present aviation policy being followed by the Government has not been
 effective in making the private airlines share the social obligations of the country.  The Committee feels that the private
 airlines have been focusing on lucrative trunk routes only.  These airlines have been operating only on the basis of
 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal
 Guidelines. The Committee recommends that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be revisited to ensure that the private
 domestic airlines also share the social obligation of connecting remote parts of the country in the true sense and not by
 merely completing the formalities in this regard.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
41.       The Route Dispersal Guidelines (RDG) issued by the Government in 1994, require all scheduled airlines to deploy at
 least 10% of the capacity deployed by them on major trunk routes (i.e. CAT-I routes) on the routes to/from North East,
 Jammu & Kashmir, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (i.e. CAT II routes). Out of the total capacity so
 deployed in CAT-II routes, 10 % of the capacity is required to be deployed for connectivity with North East, Jammu &
 Kashmir, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Further, the airlines are also required to deploy 50% of the
 capacity, deployed on CAT-I routes, on non-trunk routes i.e. CAT-III routes. The Director General of Civil Aviation
 monitors the compliance with the RDG on a monthly basis.
42.       The Government had set-up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Director General of Civil Aviation vide Order
 dated 23.9.2003 to review the existing Route Dispersal Guidelines. The Committee has   submitted its report on 18.3.2005,
 which is under active consideration of the Government. The concerns expressed by the Committee shall be duly considered
 before taking any final decision in the matter. The private airlines are also being apprised about these concerns for
 appropriate action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43.       The Committee fails to understand the nature and reasons for the inordinate delay by DGCA and that of the Ministry,
 of over nine months to come out with a specific time frame for accepting the recommendation. The Committee recommends
 that the matter be expedited with desired pace.
REQUIREMENT OF TRAINED MANPOWER
(Recommendation at Para 50)
 
44.       The Committee is of the view that as per the policy being pursued by the Government in granting licenses to new
 private airlines, a lot of investment is coming in the airline industry. Vast expansion of fleet is also taking place in the
 existing national and private carriers. The Committee feels that there is a mismatch between the pace at which the airline
 fleet is expanding and the human resource being groomed for the same thereby, resulting in tremendous shortage of trained
 manpower. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should undertake an objective assessment of the
 requirement of trained manpower for civil aviation sector as a whole in the country on priority basis.   The Committee also
 recommends that the Ministry should fix standard norms and strictly monitor the quality of training being imparted by the
 training institutes in the private sector.  Due emphasis should also be laid on Human Resource Development with focus on
 training for increasing the productivity and for providing better and customer friendly service.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
45.       The growth and expansion of the civil aviation sector has created a shortfall of trained manpower.  Ministry of Civil
 Aviation recognizes this constraint and is endeavoring to bridge the gap to the best of its ability and with the resources
 available. There is a continued emphasis on Human Resource Development as a part of on going training programmes of
 airlines which, inter-alia encompasses increase in productivity and better and more customer friendly services.
(i)        Assessment of requirement of trained manpower
46.       Whenever  any Airline/operator proposes to start operation after obtaining approval of Ministry of Civil Aviation,
 Directorate General of Civil Aviation conducts preparatory meeting to ensure the availability of the infrastructure and
 necessary manpower. If they are found equipped with necessary manpower and infrastructure, the Directorate General of
 Civil Aviation issues the “No objection certificate” for manpower for import of aircraft.
47.       Requirement of Scheduled Airlines as assessed by DGCA is at Annexure-I.

HIGH COST OF AIR TURBINE FUEL (ATF)
(Recommendations at Paras 75 and 78)
63.       Fuel plays a crucial role in the cost structure and profitability of any airline. High cost of ATF in the country
 increases the cost of operation. The Committee welcomes the proposed amendment in the Central Sales Tax Act whereby
 sales tax on bonded ATF uplifted for international operation would be exempted. The Committee is hopeful that this move
 would, to some extent, help our national carriers strengthen their financial position.  The Committee, however, is concerned
 to note that some states which had earlier taken initiative and reduced sales tax on ATF, have retracted and imposed high
 rates of sales tax on ATF.,  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Finance should consider and give approval  to the
 proposal of Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding notifying ATF as ‘Declared Good’ under Section 14 of Central Sales Tax
 Act on priority basis so that sales tax on ATF could be contained with the maximum rate of 4%. The Committee further
 recommends that the Ministry of Finance may also discuss the issue with the State Governments and try to convince them
 that the reduction in the sales tax on ATF will certainly increase the efficiency and viability of our carriers.
64.       The Committee recommends that the Government should create conditions, which provide wider choice to the airline
 companies for procurement of ATF. The Committee hopes that this step would promote competition among the suppliers
 and help lowering the rates of ATF to some extent.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
65.       ATF is a major cost component of airlines in India. It constitutes about 35% of total operating cost for domestic
 operations.
 
66.       Two reasons for high price of ATF in India are:
 
(i)   High rate of sales tax charged by State Governments on ATF sold to domestic flights.
(ii)  High marketing and distribution margins charged by Oil PSUs, which are in monopoly situation for supply of ATF.
67.       As per notification issued under section 5 of Central Sales Tax Act (CST) w.e.f. 7
th June, 2005, there would be no
 sales tax on ATF purchased for international flights of designated Indian Carrier. This would bring Indian designated carries
 at par with foreign carriers, which are already getting sales tax exemption on ATF purchase.
68.       With a view to reduce the incidence of sales tax, it has been suggested to the Finance Ministry that ATF sold to
 domestic flights may be notified as ‘Declared Goods’ under Section 14  of the Central Sales Tax Act, so as to cap the rate of
 Sales Tax on ATF to 4%. Finance Ministry has, however, informed that the proposal could not be agreed to due to serious
 revenue implications for the State Governments.  ATF sold to turbo-prop aircraft is already notified as ‘Declared Goods’
 under Section 14 of the Central Sales Tax Act attracting 4% sales tax on ATF.
69.       The State Governments may get affected only marginally by the above measure. But, these would go a long way in
 improving the health of the aviation industry in the country and ultimately fostering the economy, tourism and regional
 development to a great extent.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

 (Recommendations at Para 86)
71.       The Committee is of the view that, as brought out by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the proposals of Fringe Benefits
 Tax, if implemented on the airlines industry, would have a major financial impact on airlines operators.   The Committee is
 of the view that the elements brought out in para 84 above do not truly form part of benefits being given to the employees.  
 In fact, these are clear-cut major cost components for the functioning of airlines and should not be considered as qualifying
 factors for the imposition of Fringe Benefit Tax as proposed in the Budget.   Imposition of tax on the above stated cost
 elements would adversely affect the profitability of the airlines, which have very recently started coming out of the
 recessionary trend.   Further, the imposition of tax on aircraft repair, running and maintenance expenses (including
 depreciation) and consumption of fuel will directly raise the cost of operations.   This may result in fare increase, thereby
 making the air travel costlier.   Further, treating the main operating costs of airlines at par with fringe benefits appears to be
 illogical.    Taxing such cost is not in consonance with the basic objective of this new levy.   The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that Ministry of Finance should reconsider its decision and recognizing the peculiarity of the nature of working
 of the airlines industry, exclude the expenditure on items mentioned in para 84 above from the purview of the Fringe
 Benefits Tax.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
72.       Ministry of Finance has duly considered Airline’s plea in respect of expenditure incurred on repairs running and
 maintenance of aircraft, consumption of fuel and depreciation on aircraft. Recognizing that these are major cost components
 for functioning of airlines and in no way result in any fringe benefit to employees, these items have been removed from the
 ambit of fringe benefit tax when the bill was finally passed.
73.       The cost of free or concessional ticket for private journeys of employees or their family members and expenditure
 incurred by airlines on Crew Hotel accommodation and foreign travel expenses has not been removed from the purview of
 FBT. The free and concessional tickets provided to employees is on a ‘subject to load’ basis and are made available to the
 employees in accordance with the IATA Resolutions. As per the provisions of FBT, the valuation of these tickets has to be
 made at a value at which these tickets are offered to the public. It is very relevant that such tickets cannot be offered to the
 public and hence such tickets have no market value. Therefore, the value of such free concessional tickets is not
 determinable. It may be pertinent to mention that the airline employees are provided seats on a subject to availability basis
 and that to at the last moment that is prior to departure of the flight.  Where the business of the enterprise itself is carriage of
 passengers and where such enterprise does not provide any LTC facility to its employees, such free concessional tickets
 should be outside the purview of FBT.
74.       In the course of conduct of the business, the crew is required to travel in the aircraft and stay in hotel which is a
 necessity in course of their flight duties and it cannot be stated that benefit accrues to the crew out of such travel and stay at
 hotel. Considering the peculiar nature of the airline business, crew hotel expenses and foreign travel expenses in case of
 airlines needs to be excluded from the purview of FBT.
75.       The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance.

MODERNISATION AND RETRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
(Recommendation at Para 99)
81.       The Committee is constrained to note that the decision to modernize Delhi and Mumbai airports was initiated in the
 year 2000 and till now, the Government has not been able to come out with any concrete plans in this regard.  The
 Committee is dissatisfied to note that the Ministry has made different cost estimate at different stages and there exists a huge
 difference in the figures quoted by the Ministry.  The Committee also regrets to note that the Ministry has not considered the
 alternate proposal submitted by the AAI Employees Joint Forum on the modernisation of Mumbai and Delhi Airports.   The
 Committee is surprised to find as to why the Government has not updated the proposal submitted by the Airports Authority
 of India in the year 2000 to effect modernisation and feels that the proposal should be implemented.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
82.       The Government had decided to restructure in the year 2000 the four metro airports of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and
 Kolkata through leasing route.  However, the legal process for introducing a suitable amendment in the AAI Act, 1994 could
 be finalised in 2003.  In the meantime, the Government had reviewed the process and it was decided in September, 2003 to
 restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through Joint Venture Route (JVR).  The Government has made substantial progress
 in the matter. Nine consortia of bidders had been short listed on the basis of Expression of Interest (EOI).  They have already
 been issued Request for Proposal (RFP) document and draft of other transaction documents on 01.04.2005.  These Pre
 Qualified Bidders (PQBs) were given 12 weeks of time to submit their technical and financial bids which has since been
 extended because of inter ministerial consultation process in taking decisions on some key issues raised by PQBs etc.    The
 cost estimates have been made by the Global Technical Advisor appointed by AAI (which does not include cost on account
 relocation of the existing assets and for removal of encroachment).

 and Mumbai airports respectively (at current prices) over a 20-year development plan period.
84.       A broad concept of alternate plan submitted by AAI Employees Joint Forum was examined by a Committee of AAI
 officers constituted for this purpose under the chairmanship of Member (Finance), AAI.  It was found that the concept of
 alternate plan submitted by the forum was very sketchy in nature and incomplete in many aspects and therefore needed to be
 developed into a comprehensive alternate plan.  Since October, 2004, a number of meetings have been held between
 members of Joint Forum, Financial Consultants and the constituted Committee during which clarifications and other inputs
 desired by the Joint Forum were furnished. However, no comprehensive alternate plan has been furnished as yet by the Joint
 Forum for examination of the Committee.

 Mumbai airports were not processed in view of the fact that a decision for restructuring of four metro airports through

 is expected to be carried out by the Joint Venture Companies after the restructuring of these airports, as per the provisions in

 Parliament on the  23
rd August 2005.

 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
