R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the observations/ recommendations as
 contained in its Ninetieth Report on  “Development of Airport Sector with Special Emphasis on new Modern Airports”, which was presented to both
 the Houses of Parliament on 23rd August, 2005.
 2.         Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 18 th November, 2005 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been categorised as follows: -
(i)         Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
              Para Nos.: 51, 65                                                                                                    Total- 2
(ii)        Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry’s replies:
Para Nos.:  Nil                                                                                                       Total- Nil
(iii)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos.: 43, 49, 54, 56, 61                                                                                    Total- 5
(iv)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are still awaited:
Para Nos.:  20, 21, 26, 31, 46, 62, 70, 82, 86, 90                                                    Total- 10
3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee
 should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the
 Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Ninetieth Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry, and
 recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
(Recommendation at Para 20)
 
5.         The Committee is constrained to note that the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports has been
 lingering on for a fairly long period and still the Government has not been able to come up with any concrete plans in this regard.  The Ministry of
 Civil Aviation has also not been able to even firm up the financial requirements for these projects.  The Government has been quoting different cost
 estimates at different stage.  The Committee also notes that the initial figures of Rs.10, 000 crore to Rs.20, 000 crore stated by the Secretary of the
 Ministry were too inflated and also gave the impression that the money was required immediately in one go which in fact was actually required in
 phases spread over 15 to 20 years.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         Union Cabinet took decision in the year 2000 to restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through long term lease.  However, while the process
 went along, it was found that AAI Act needed amendment to enable the process to move through long term lease route. The Government took steps
 to amend the AAI Act 1994.  It took nearly three and half Years to carry the amendment.  Finally the amendment was approved by the Parliament in
 July 2003.  The Union Cabinet in Sept 2003 decided to restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through JV route involving leasing of assets. 
 Accordingly an Empowered Group of Ministers was appointed.  After undertaking extensive due diligence at various levels now the modernization
 and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports is at the final stage.  The technical and financial bids have been received on 14.9.2005 and are at
 evaluation stage. The Government has a well determined mode and plan of the process of modernization of these airports.
 
7.         The delay in this process has been mainly on account of legal problems, in-depth and intense Inter-ministerial consultations as this transaction
 was first of its kind both in terms of scope and complexity.  The airports are to be developed by the Joint Venture Company (JVC) which will
 necessarily have a world class airport operator. Apart from executing the mandated capital expenditure within 2 and 5 years of the effective date, the
 JVC will have to adhere to the initial development plan submitted at the time of bidding and the Master Plan to be submitted to the Govt. within six
 months of the signing of the agreement.

8.         The variance in cost estimates occurred because they have been furnished at different points of time when the Global Technical Adviser was
 still working on its report. Capital expenditure is to be carried out over a period of 20 years broken into 4 stages of 5 year each and linked with the
 traffic trigger with substantial capital expenditure envisaged in Phase I i.e. 2005 to 2009. The estimates do not include the expenditure to be incurred
 by AAI for modernizing the ATC etc.  It also does not include expenditure which could be incurred by other public agencies for instance, Delhi
 Metro, NHAI, Delhi Water Supply, BSES, etc.  Further, nothing prevents JVC to incur more expenditure if it is warranted by the expected traffic.
 More traffic would mean more revenue and therefore there would be incentive for JVC to enhance capacity to get more traffic. If traffic trigger
 requires early and heavier investment, the JVC is incentivised to undertake the investment accordingly. In the light of the above even the initial
 figures of Rs.10000 to Rs.20000 crore for both the airports may not be unrealistic. This figure is less than the investment incurred at other
 international airports with world class standards. It has been estimated that the capital investment to the extent of Rs.7961 crores and Rs.6131 crores
 will be required for Delhi and Mumbai airports, respectively over a period of 20 years in phases.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
9.         The Committee is not convinced with the reply put forth by the Ministry and observes that clear-cut statistics with regard to modernization of
 airports should be given to the public and the Parliament.  As the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports
 involves huge expenditure and also determines the future of aviation sector in this country, the exaggerated initial cost estimates indicate poor
 financial planning.  The Committee feels that the unrealistic cost estimates at the planning stage might have swayed the decision in favour of the
 Joint Venture route. 
 (Recommendation at Para 21)
10.       The Committee feels that the process of modernization as explained by the Ministry, is very slow and the target to be achieved is also minimal
 in terms of global standards.  The Committee observes that Airport Authority of India at present has already achieved the target with the present rate
 of investment.  The Committee does not agree with the Ministry of Civil Aviation that resource crunch is the main reason for inviting private sector
 participation for the modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports.  The quantum of investment which is to the tune of Rs.13, 786
 crore, required for modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports is not on the higher side and that too is required in a manner over a period of 15 to
 20 years.  The Committee feels that the Government can even mobilize the funds required.  This will ensure not only the management control of the
 proposed operators of the airports in the hands of Indian nationals but also result in protecting the safety, security and sovereignty of the country.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 11.      The decision to restructure and modernize airports through PPP route is a widely prevalent public policy tool and is not primarily dictated by
 the resource crunch faced by the Government. The intention is to have world class airport and world class management with the world class airport
 operator under public private partnership. While Government can mobilize the funds such funds are more needed to be used for supporting social
 sector development programmes such as health, education, social welfare, etc. In the airport sector if private investment can come it would be
 endeavour of the Government to facilitate that as the public investment saved here could be used elsewhere where it is more required such as North
 East etc.
 
12.       The airports at Delhi and Mumbai shall be managed by the JVC which will be registered in India under the Companies Act and therefore will
 function under the Indian Companies Act.  This JVC shall have the right to operate and manage the airports as per the transaction agreements singed
 within the ambit of laws of India, e.g., Indian Contract Act, Indian Arbitration Act and other applicable laws. The safety shall continue to be the
 responsibility of DGCA and there is no dilution in its authority. Security shall be the responsibility of State and there is no dilution in its
 responsibility as far as airport operated by JVC is concerned.
 
13.       In the JVC maximum FDI, which is permitted, is only 49%.  Thus, the management control of these airports remain in the hands of Indian
 nationals.  However the management of these airports is sought to be improved by involving world class airport operators in the JVC. Given the
 above the development of metro airports through the JVC route does not, in any way, compromise on safety, security and sovereignty of the country.
 In fact, the ownership of assets remain with the AAI / Govt.
 
14.       As regards performance standards, Government is aiming to achieve average global standard of 3.75
 with the aim of ultimately attaining
 standard of 4 (The highest standard of world being 4.45).  The current standards at these airports are much below the world standards. Earlier, AAI
 did not undertake survey of these airports through IATA.  This has been commissioned from January 2005 on quarterly basis.  As per the latest
 survey from April – June 2005, the average at Delhi and Mumbai airports is 2.94 and 3.06 respectively.  In case of Mumbai, the average has declined
 from 3.20 to 3.06 as recorded from Jan – March 2005 whereas at Delhi, there is a slight improvement.  It may be mentioned that survey of one or two
 quarter is not enough to judge the attainment of standards and linking with investments. In fact, the standards coveredunder IATA survey are directly
 related with the management of facilities. In this respect, AAI’s management leaves much to be desired.  AAI does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency pointed out in the survey as there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for
 non-attainment of standards as against the JVC which will have penalties for the non-attainment of the same. This could even lead to termination of
 the agreement.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
15.       The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry.  The Committee is not convinced that the Government cannot
 mobilise the funds for executing the modernisation plan of Delhi and Mumbai airports on its own as the estimated quantum of investment is required
 over a period of 15 to 20 years.   Moreover, the modernisation plan for the Mumbai airport cannot address the situation beyond the year 2014. The
 Committee therefore recommends that the Government should reconsider its plans to privatise Delhi and Mumbai airports under the garb of
 modernisation and instead give a serious consideration to the workable alternate plan suggested by Airports Authority of India Employees Joint
 Forum. The Committee also recommends that the Government should immediately initiate the groundwork for Greenfield Airports in Delhi and
 Mumbai with public-private participation.  
 
16.       As regards performance standards, the Committee is sad to note that even today the Airports Authority of India does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency, as pointed out in the survey conducted by IATA regarding performance standards, and

 there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for non-attainment of standards.  It indicates that due to lack of provision of imposing
 penalty/liquidated damage on Airports Authority of India for non-attainment of standards, AAI could not fulfill consumer satisfaction and meet
 international norms and standards. The Committee feels that this needs to be corrected.  In an era of globalisation, a major profit making PSU like the
 Airports Authority of India cannot function in an isolated manner in the aviation sector.  There should not be any compromise in terms of consumer
 satisfaction and overall compliance to international norms and standards.  Both Airports Authority of India and any other private sector entrant
 through JV route should be treated at par.  The Committee fails to understand that if Airports Authority of India lacks adequate mechanism to cure
 deficiencies and is not conforming to international performance standards, then how it is handling all other airports in the country.
 
(Recommendation at Para 26)
 
17.       The Committee notes that the Government intends to attract investment worth Rs.5825 crore spread over a period of 15 years for the
 modernization and restructuring of Mumbai airport.    The Committee has been informed by the Ministry that there is no scope of having a second
 runway at Mumbai airport which could be helpful in terms of air operations.  Further, the passenger traffic movement is also expected to go up from
 14 million in 2004 to 52 million in 2024.  The Committee also understands that by 2012, Mumbai airport would get absolute chocked.  However, the
 development plans of Ministry of Civil Aviation for Mumbai Airports goes beyond 2012 i.e. upto 2019.  The Committee fails to understand as to
 how the huge investment to be made at the airport could be justified when the existing capacity constrains would not permit capacity addition.  The
 Committee is of the opinion that modernization is not merely about the creation of facilities, expansion of the terminal buildings and putting up fancy
 malls at the airports.  It should rather increase the capacity of the airports to handle more flights, by construction of additional runways, which is
 certainly not a probability in the case of Mumbai airport.  The Committee feels that if international flights have to move around on the skies for half-
an-hour to forty-five minutes after having reached the destination, then there could be no commensurate return as far as the investment, increase in
 the number of aircraft and the number of passengers actually traveling to the airport are concerned.  The Committee is of the firm view that investing
 huge money on modernization of Mumbai airport would be waste.  The Committee is of the opinion that there are certain inherent technological
 constrains while reconstructing an existing structure, particularly in the case of Mumbai airport and the option of going in for a new Greenfield
 airport rather than proposed modernization of Mumbai airport will be more prudent.  However, some investment towards augmenting the capacity
 will have to be made to address the immediate exigencies of the situation at least till such time a new Greenfield airport comes into operation.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should rather go in for construction of a new Greenfield airport with much more capacity at
 Mumbai which would require much less investment and the efforts in this direction should begin at the earliest.  In such case both the Greenfield and
 the existing airport can compete with each other.  The Committee is also of the opinion that given the growth of aviation sector in country, the
 existing infrastructure at Delhi airport also possesses that inherent lacuna and is therefore, inadequate to handle the growth being projected for the
 future by the Government.  The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of having a Greenfield airport in Delhi
 also.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
18.      Global Technical Adviser (GTA)’s report on airfield capacity of Mumbai states as follows:
 
(i)
                  With enhanced taxiways and enhanced ATC procedures, the existing runway could accommodate projected traffic to between 2009
 and 2014.
(ii)                With some increase in average aircraft size, the existing runway, with enhanced taxiway and ATC procedures could accommodate
 projected traffic to beyond 2014.
(iii)               A close spaced parallel runway could accommodate projected traffic levels to about 2019.
(iv)              To achieve the 20 year forecast traffic a wide spaced parallel runway would be required.
(v)                Achievement of high capacity figures is dependent on several factors, including some controlled by others (e.g. ATC, airlines). This
 will occur through gradual development over future years.
 
19.       Setting up of a runway at (iii) above requires relocation of hangars of AI, additional land and removal of obstacles in the approach pathways,
 where heavy public investment will be needed besides practical difficulties. Action at (iv) is also not practical. Action at (ii) above will add capacity
 by 50% and last to meet demand upto 2014 and beyond. Thus, the existing airport will have to cater to the traffic upto 2014. Capacity on the airside
 and terminal will need to be created to cater to the traffic upto 2014 and beyond.  The capacity on the airside will be added by taxiways, ATC
 procedures and terminal expansions, etc.  These facilities will remain at the existing airport.  Hence the investment made on these capacity will not
 be a waste but will be used by the existing airport for future.
 
20.       As regards a Greenfield airport at Mumbai, there is a proposal at planning stage for setting up a second airport linked with the above traffic
 trigger and other constraints.  As regard Delhi, the present airport can be developed to meet traffic requirement upto 80 million passengers. Hence, it
 is felt that there is no need for second Greenfield airport in Delhi immediately. There is a huge difference between the cost of incremental capacity at
 a Brownfield Airport and the cost of creating the same capacity through the Greenfield Airport. As long as the capacity is not optimized at the
 Brownfield airport, foregoing the option of creation of additional capacity at the Brownfield Airport and setting up a Greenfield Airport will not be
 prudent.
 
21.       At Mumbai airport there is still significant scope for optimizing the capacity through physical, technological and managerial improvements. 
 By undertaking improved ATC procedures, taxiways etc. the aircraft movement can increase from present 25-26 to 40-42 per hour i.e. an increase of
 60% (approx.). Parallel or two runways not necessarily generate adequate capacity if well designed taxi ways and parking bays do not co-exist.
 
22.       However there could be different drivers for decision to develop Greenfield Airport and decision could be taken in future based on the then
 available requirements. A Right of First Refusal (ROFR) is proposed to be provided to the existing airport operator at Delhi / Mumbai for the second
 airport subject to the following conditions.
 
(i)
                  The second airport will not be set up before the trigger point in terms of traffic growth has occurred.
 
(ii)
                Approval process for second airport may begin five years or even earlier before the trigger point is likely to be reached.

(iii)               JVC need not be consulted in development of the proposal of the second airport due to conflict of interest.
 
(iv)              The shareholding restriction to which the ROFR is tied may be removed and instead provide that the approval of AAI for change of
 shareholding and airport operator will be required.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
23.       The Committee notes that in the assessment report of the Global Technical Advisor (GTA) on airfield capacity of Mumbai airport, it has been
 stated that with enhanced taxiways and enhanced ATC procedures, the existing runway could accommodate projected traffic to between 2009 and
 2014.  Moreover, with some increase in average aircraft size, the existing runway, with enhanced taxiway and ATC procedures could accommodate

24.       The Committee observes that there is a contradiction in the stand of the Ministry as they first agreed that there was no scope for any further

 air-operations.  The position now informed by the Ministry is that "There is a huge difference between the cost of incremental capacity at a

 developing this particular airport at Gaya, Airports Authority of India will also earn some revenue.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that some
 via media should be evolved and the Airports Authority of India Board should reconsider its stand to acquire 101 acres of land from the Government

MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
            The Committee is not convinced with the reply put forth by the Ministry and observes that clear-cut statistics with regard to modernization of
 airports should be given to the public and the Parliament.  As the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports
 involves huge expenditure and also determines the future of aviation sector in this country, the exaggerated initial cost estimates indicate poor
 financial planning.  The Committee feels that the unrealistic cost estimates at the planning stage might have swayed the decision in favour of the
 Joint Venture route.   (Para 9)
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry.  The Committee is not convinced that the Government cannot
 mobilise the funds for executing the modernisation plan of Delhi and Mumbai airports on its own as the estimated quantum of investment is required
 over a period of 15 to 20 years.   Moreover, the modernisation plan for the Mumbai airport cannot address the situation beyond the year 2014. The
 Committee therefore recommends that the Government should reconsider its plans to privatise Delhi and Mumbai airports under the garb of
 modernisation and instead give a serious consideration to the workable alternate plan suggested by Airports Authority of India Employees Joint
 Forum. The Committee also recommends that the Government should immediately initiate the groundwork for Greenfield Airports in Delhi and
 Mumbai with public-private participation.   (Para 15)
 
            As regards performance standards, the Committee is sad to note that even today the Airports Authority of India does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency, as pointed out in the survey conducted by IATA regarding performance standards, and
 there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for non-attainment of standards.  It indicates that due to lack of provision of imposing
 penalty/liquidated damage on Airports Authority of India for non-attainment of standards, AAI could not fulfill consumer satisfaction and meet
 international norms and standards. The Committee feels that this needs to be corrected.  In an era of globalisation, a major profit making PSU like the
 Airports Authority of India cannot function in an isolated manner in the aviation sector.  There should not be any compromise in terms of consumer
 satisfaction and overall compliance to international norms and standards.  Both Airports Authority of India and any other private sector entrant
 through JV route should be treated at par.  The Committee fails to understand that if Airports Authority of India lacks adequate mechanism to cure
 deficiencies and is not conforming to international performance standards, then how it is handling all other airports in the country. (Para 16)
 
            The Committee notes that in the assessment report of the Global Technical Advisor (GTA) on airfield capacity of Mumbai airport, it has been
 stated that with enhanced taxiways and enhanced ATC procedures, the existing runway could accommodate projected traffic to between 2009 and
 2014.  Moreover, with some increase in average aircraft size, the existing runway, with enhanced taxiway and ATC procedures could accommodate
 projected traffic to beyond 2014 and to achieve the 20 year forecast traffic, a wide spaced parallel runway would be required.  In brief, the Ministry
 is of the opinion that the existing airport will cater to traffic upto 2014 and that capacity on the airside and terminal will need to be created to cater to
 traffic upto 2014 and beyond.  (Para 23)
 
            The Committee observes that there is a contradiction in the stand of the Ministry as they first agreed that there was no scope for any further
 development on the airside at Mumbai airport since there was no scope of having a second runway at that airport which could be helpful in terms of
 air-operations.  The position now informed by the Ministry is that "There is a huge difference between the cost of incremental capacity at a
 Brownfield Airport and the cost of creating the same capacity through the Greenfield Airport. As long as the capacity is not optimized at the
 Brownfield airport, foregoing the option of creation of additional capacity at the Brownfield Airport and setting up a Greenfield Airport will not be
 prudent".(Para 24)
 
           The Committee feels that the Ministry is keeping the Committee half informed as they are now saying that "parallel or two runways not
 necessarily generate adequate capacity if well designed taxi ways and parking bays do not co-exist".   The Committee has not been informed about
 the present scheme of things and the proposed modernization programme to be undertaken in the immediate future at Mumbai/Delhi airports by the
 private sector and how much capacity is estimated to be added and whether there will be newly designed taxi ways and parking bays.     (Para 25)
 
           The Committee desires that the Ministry should atleast now apprise it clearly about (a) the traffic and cargo expected to increase in future in
 the normal course on five yearly basis; the capacity addition with modifications in the existing Brownfield airports in Mumbai and Delhi through
 modernization under JV route; (b) the expected increase in traffic/cargo after modernization of Mumbai and Delhi airports; (c) the cost estimation of
 Greenfield airports at Mumbai/Delhi and the capacity of those airports in terms of time period vis-à-vis traffic and cargo to be handled; and (d) the
 difference in the cost of modernization of the existing Brownfield airports and construction of new Greenfield airports.  (Para 26)
 
           The Committee is of the opinion that without a proper assessment, it will be myopic to conclude that there is no immediate need of Greenfield
 airports at Mumbai and Delhi.  The Ministry has not even estimated as to when the trigger point will occur in terms of traffic growth to justify the
 new Greenfield airports in these metro cities. It is surprising to note that even at the planning stage, the Ministry is proposing to provide a Right of
 First Refusal (ROFR) for the second airport to the airport operator at Delhi / Mumbai, thereby favouring JV route. The existing plans therefore may
 lead to a situation wherein both the existing as well as the second airports at Delhi/Mumbai will be under the management control of private
 operators.(Para 27)
 
           The Committee is also of the opinion that the Ministry should reconsider its present plan on the modernisation and restructuring of Delhi and
 Mumbai Airports keeping in view the current scenario of the domestic as well as international aviation sector.  The present plan will only create
 monopoly in Delhi and Mumbai.  The Ministry has turned a blind eye to the paradigm shift which is occurring in South East Asian and East Asian
 countries where the focus is on the development of both Greenfield and Brownfield airports together, serving the dual purpose of enhancing the
 capacity and providing healthy competition in the best interests of the aviation sector. (Para 28)
 
           The Committee notes carefully the assurance given by the Ministry that "AAI will be better off as during the period 2006-2024 the present
 value of cash flow would be Rs.1286.5 crores where as if status quo is maintained then there could be a negative present value of cash flow to AAI at
 Rs.  (-) 998.89 crore" and "post restructuring AAI will not only be able to maintain other airports in the country but also upgrade and modernize
 these airports".  However, the Committee reiterates its observations/recommendations that the Ministry should review its strategy for the
 modernisation and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.   (Para 37)

GREENFIELD AIRPORTS AT BANGALORE AND HYDERABAD
 
            The Committee is not convinced by the reply furnished by the Ministry on the Greenfield Airport at Bangalore.   It is clear from the reply that
 the clause regarding the operation of the EPC Contracts by the Joint Venture Partners did not exist in the initial International Bidding Process. The
 issue of EPC contracts was settled between the shortlisted bidders at a later stage that too at the instance of such bidders.  The Committee notes that
 the deviation from the transparent competitive bidding process can be resorted only in exceptional cases.  The Committee finds that the Ministry has
 not justified the existence of exceptional circumstances in the award of EPC contracts at BIAL to Joint Venture Partners (JVPs).  Therefore, it is
 fallacious to contend that the procedure adopted for selection of the JVP being in itself a bidding process, it is a valid ground for not adopting a
 bidding process for the realization and operation of the project.  The Committee is therefore of the opinion that the further procedures evolved in
 respect of EPC contracts do not cure the inherent lacuna in the award of such contracts to JVPs.   Moreover, the justification sought by the Ministry
 on the issue by quoting similar instances of award of EPC contracts to strategic investors in other projects by other Ministries cannot be accepted.  
 The Ministry had earlier denied the existence of the award of EPC contracts to JVPs at BIAL before the Committee and the present justification is
 merely an afterthought, if not an outright attempt to mislead the Committee.  The Committee notes that the Ministry has now issued detailed
 guidelines in this regard to all State Governments for compliance in future.   The Committee however, reiterates its recommendation that a proper
 enquiry should be conducted into the entire matter by an independent agency as to why the provision of awarding EPC by competitive mode was
 missing in the case of BIAL.   (Para 65)
 
            The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.  The Committee recommends that it should be apprised about the details of the financial
 modalities adopted in the case of Hyderabad Airport.  (Para 68)
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply.  The Committee in its Report on the ATR furnished by the Ministry on the
 recommendations/observations made in the 88
th Report has recommended that the Government should reconsider the decision to close down the
 existing airport at Hyderabad on the commissioning of a new International airport.  The recommendation is reproduced below: -
“The aviation sector in the country has changed dramatically with the low cost carriers gaining ground.   The previously unviable routes are
 now proving to be profitable ones and there is stiff competition amongst the private operators to extend their reach to all parts of the country.  In this
 changed scenario, instead of reassessing its strategy, the Ministry is following the unhealthy policy of creation of monopoly by promoting only one
 airport at different metros, as in the case of Delhi and Mumbai. The Committee also notes that the justification put forward by the Ministry for the
 closure of the existing airport at Hyderabad is contrary to the rationale of the Ministry for rejecting the proposals for Greenfield airports at Delhi and
 Mumbai.  In respect of those two airports, the Ministry has maintained throughout that unless the capacity is not optimized or added in the existing
 Brownfield airport, it is not prudent to set up a Greenfield airport.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Government should reconsider the
 decision to close down the existing airport at Hyderabad on the commissioning of a new International airport.”  (Para 71)
 
            The Committee observes that the Government is considering the question of waiver of condition of dependence of budgetary support in view
 of the special circumstances where AAI has to maintain certain airports irrespective of commercial viability and appointment of non-official
 directors on the board.  The Committee hopes that Airports Authority of India will be given the status of 'Mini Ratna' at the earliest so that it gets
 adequate opportunity to utilize its professional excellence in the area of development and maintenance of airports in the country and recommends
 that the process be expedited.  (Para 75)

UNDER UTILISATION OF ILS CAT-III SYSTEM INSTALLED AT INDIRA GANDHI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, DELHI
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply. In this connection, the Committee would like to invite the attention of the Ministry towards the
 recommendation made in the Report on ATR furnished by the Ministry on the observations/ recommendations contained in the 88 th Report, which is
 reproduced below: -
“The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry and feels vindicated by the developments during the fog this winter.  The
 massive disruption of flights into and out of Delhi has highlighted the gross underutilization of the costly ILS CAT-III system installed at Indira
 Gandhi International Airport.  This has resulted in the non-utilisation of the expenditure from the tax payers’ money.  It appears that the different
 airlines resort to diversion of flights instead of using the available infrastructure because it is economical for them to follow such practice rather than
 training the pilots on CAT-III system.   The Committee feels that whatever be the reasons, the passenger facilities should be paramount and they
 should not be put to any hardship.  Moreover, even if IA and AI have trained their pilots and are using the system, the diversion of flights of the
 private carriers gives adverse publicity to the civil aviation sector as a whole.  The Committee feels that there should be some penal provision to
 discourage the diversion of flights due to fog by the private operators or they should be compelled to utilise the ILS CAT-III system. The Committee
 takes note of the relevant news reports appearing in the print and visual media and the inadequate response of the Ministry thereon. The Committee
 also notes that the Ministry is now waking up to the need for the implementation of the recommendation in the face of severe public criticism. The
 Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the extreme foggy conditions, training
 of pilots should be made compulsory by the private airlines on CAT-III System.  The Committee further recommends that utilization of CAT-II and
 CAT-III systems by private airlines should be made compulsory by training a fixed minimum proportion of their pilots and it should be enforced by
 the Government strictly.” (Para 105)

R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
 observations/recommendations contained in its Eighty-third Report on the “Functioning of the Commission of Railway
 Safety”, which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on the 6 th December, 2004 and laid on the table of Lok Sabha on 3rd
 December, 2004.
 
 2.         Action Taken Replies on some of the observations/recommendations contained in the Report were received
 from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 26
th May, 2005 and it was informed that the complete Action Taken Replies on

 the Report would be forwarded on the receipt of the views/comments of the Ministry of Railways on the issues related
 to them. Accordingly, the Action Taken Replies on the remaining observations/ recommendations were received from
 the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 5 th January, 2006. The Action Taken Replies received from the Government in
 respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report, have been categorised as follows: -
 (i)         Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Government:
              Para Nos.:  21, 27, 37, 60, 63, 67  and 72                                                  Total - 7
(ii)        Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government
 replies:
Para No.: 69                                                                                                 Total - 1
(iii)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted by the
 Committee:
Para No.: 71                                                                                                 Total - 1
(iv)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are still awaited:
Para Nos.: 32 and 52                                                                                    Total - 2
3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as
 interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee  has made observations on each item of Action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Eighty-third
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government, and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
APPOINTMENT TO THE CADRE OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
(Recommendation at Para 21)
5.         The Committee is of the opinion that the mandate of Ministry of Civil Aviation is altogether different from the
 mandate of the Commission of Railway Safety. Therefore, the Ministry of Civil Aviation is not in a position to address
 the administrative problems of the Commission of Railway Safety adequately. In order to ensure the impartial working
 of the Commission of Railway Safety, it is essential that the Commission works outside the control of both the
 Ministries of Railways and Civil Aviation. In order to make the functioning of the Commission more effective, it is
 strongly felt that the Commission should be provided greater powers and independence. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Commission of Railway Safety should be made an autonomous statutory body like Election
 Commission and Union Public Service Commission. The Committee also agrees with the contention of the Ministry of
 Railways that officers below the rank of Commissioner of Railway Safety should also not be sent on deputation, rather
 they should go on absorption terms to the Commission. The Committee is of the firm view that this would make the
 Commission independent, powerful and vigilant to the fullest extent. This would definitely go a long way in dispelling
 the general impression that the Ministry of Railways unduly influences the Commission in its functioning as it is rightly
 said that justice should not only be done but it should also appear to have been done.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.         The Commission of Railway Safety is presently placed under the administrative control of the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation. The rationale behind the separation of Railway Inspectorate (as was known earlier) was consequent to the
 recommendations of the Pacific Loco Committee 1939 that “Senior Government Inspectors of Railways should be
 placed under the administrative control of some authority other than the Railway Board”. Consequently, the
 Inspectorate was placed under the Department of Post and Air in May, 1941 and continuously thereafter under
 whichever Ministry that has held the portfolio of Civil Aviation. Thus, the Commission has always remained with the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation independent of Ministry of Railways, but for a brief period between 1985 and 1989 when the
 Department of Railways and Department of Civil Aviation were the part of Transport Ministry.
7.         The issue of placing the Commission of Railway Safety under the Ministry other than the Ministry of Railways,
 which is the safety controlling authority in respect of rail based transport operation, has been considered by the various
 high level committees including Appointments Committee of the Cabinet on different occasions and there has been
 unanimity on the views that the Commission should remain outside the control of Ministry of Railways for ensuring its
 independence.
8.         The present arrangement of the Commission of Railway Safety being placed under the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation has been working satisfactorily since May, 1967. Incidentally the ACC had decided in 1998 to maintain the
 status quo on the subject. Irrespective of the Ministry with which the Commission is attached with, the mandate of the

98thReport of Committeeon Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/98threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:11:25]
 concerned Ministry will always be different than the Commission.
9.         As regards the recommendation of the Committee on making the Commission an autonomous statutory body
 like Election Commission and Union Public Service Commission, it is submitted that a proposal in this regard is
 already under consideration in the Ministry.
 10.      Regarding the Committee’s view to have officers below the rank of Commissioner of Railway Safety on
 absorption terms rather than on deputation, it is pertinent to mention that the present set up does not provide enough
 avenues of further advancement in the Commission because the scale of pay of Dy. Commissioners is much lower than
 that of the Commissioners, the next higher grade/post available in the Commission. It is, therefore, doubtful whether
 the Railway officers would be willing to join the Commission as Dy. Commissioners on absorption basis.
 
11.       Moreover, the statutory powers are vested in the Commissioner of Railway Safety who comes from the Railways
 on permanent transfer/absorption basis. The Dy. Commissioners have no statutory powers and they assist the
 Commissioners and Chief Commissioner in their field of technical expertise. As such there is no impediment in the
 independent functioning of the Commission even if the Dy. Commissioners are taken on deputation from the Railways.
 It does not in any way influence the Commission in its functioning.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12.       The recommendation of the Committee was aimed at making the Commission of Railway Safety function
 effectively with greater powers and independence and to enhance its confidence and credibility by dispelling the
 general impression that it is influenced by the Ministry of Railways. The Ministry has on the one hand claimed that the
 present arrangement of the Commission of Railway Safety being placed under the Ministry of Civil Aviation has been
 working satisfactorily since May, 1967 but on the other it has been stated that the present set up does not provide
 enough avenues to middle level officers for further advancement in the Commission, thereby railway officers would be
 unwilling to join the Commission on absorption basis. The Committee finds these submissions contradictory. The
 Committee, however, notes that a proposal on making the Commission an autonomous body like Election Commission
 / Union Public Service Commission is under consideration. The Committee recommends that the said proposal should
 be expedited within a fixed timeframe and it should also include the aspect of comprehensive cadre review so that the
 impartiality and independence of the Commission is ensured. 
       
EFFECTIVENESS OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
(Recommendation at Para 27)
13.       The Committee is of the view that although the recommendations of the Commission of Railway Safety are not
 mandatory for the Ministry of Railways yet the situation brought out by the Commission of Railway Safety is highly
 unsatisfactory. The Committee is of the view that the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway Safety
 should receive utmost importance from the Ministry of Railways. The Committee takes exception to the fact that, on
 certain occasions, the Ministry of Railways neither consults the Commission of Railway Safety before rejecting a
 recommendation nor furnishes reasons for not accepting the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway
 Safety. The Committee strongly feels that the Commission of Railway Safety is a watchdog on behalf of the public at
 large. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Railways, should honour the commitment made by
 them to the Appointment Committee of Cabinet regarding consulting the Commission before rejecting a
 recommendation. The Committee further recommends that it should be made mandatory for the Railway
 Administration not to reject or overrule any recommendations made by the Commissioners without a meeting between
 the Chairman, Railway Board and the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, where the matters can be discussed
 threadbare and agreements reached. The Committee further recommends that while expressing their inability to accept
 the recommendations, the Railway Board should give detailed reasons for not accepting the recommendations. The
 Committee also recommends that any decision taken by the Railway Board in consultation with the Commission of
 Railway Safety must not be revoked unilaterally by the Railway Board or Zonal Railway, without prior consultation
 and approval of the Commission.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
14.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation forwarded a copy of the recommendation made by the Committee to the Railway
 Board for their comments. The remarks of the Ministry of Railways and the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on
 the remarks of the Ministry of Railways are given below: -
 
15.       Remarks of Ministry of Railways:  The recommendations made by the Commission are examined by the
 concerned Railways and in Railway Board from all angles thoroughly.  The recommendations are generally accepted

98thReport of Committeeon Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/98threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:11:25]
 and instructions are issued to Zonal Railways accordingly.  If any recommendation is not found  feasible for
 acceptance, decision in this regard is taken at appropriate level and reasons thereof are communicated to the
 Commission of Railway Safety.  There is regular interaction between Railway Board and the Commission of Railway
 Safety regarding recommendations by the latter.  Making it mandatory for the Railway Board not to reject or overrule
 any recommendation runs counter to the basic principle of authority being commensurate with the responsibility.
 
16.       Views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the remarks of the Ministry of Railways: It is agreed that final
 decision to accept or reject a recommendation made by the Commission rests with the Ministry of Railways but
 discussion with Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety before rejecting his recommendation is a fair observation made
 by the Committee.  Similarly if a recommendation of the Commission has been accepted by the Ministry of Railways it
 should not be revoked/diluted subsequently without discussion with Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety.  Ministry
 of Civil Aviation is therefore in agreement with the recommendations made by the Committee.  The Ministry of
 Railways is being requested to adhere to the recommendations of the Standing Committee as also the earlier
 commitment made by the Ministry of Railways on this count.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17.       The Committee notes that the Ministry of Railways has stated that the recommendations made by the
 Commission of Railway Safety are generally accepted and if any recommendation is not found feasible for acceptance,
 reasons thereof are communicated to the Commission.  They have further stated that there is regular interaction
 between Railway Board and the Commission of Railway Safety regarding recommendations by the latter. In this
 connection, the Commission had earlier informed the Committee that the Ministry of Railways had made a
 commitment before the Appointments Committee of Cabinet in 1998 that in case the Railways had any reservation on
 any recommendation, the same is discussed with the Commission before a final decision is taken. It was also informed
 by the Commission that with the passage of time, the Ministry of Railways has changed their stand and no discussions
 are held with the Commission on any serious issue raised by it. The Committee therefore feels that the present
 comments of the Ministry of Railways are misleading when it states that there is regular interaction with the
 Commission on their recommendations. The Committee therefore reiterates its recommendations that the Ministry of
 Railways shouldnot reject or overrule any recommendation made by the Commission without a meeting between the
 Chairman, Railway Board and the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety or without giving detailed reasons for not
 accepting the recommendations and that any decision taken by the Railway Board in consultation with the Commission
 of Railway Safety must not be revoked unilaterally by the Railway Board or Zonal Railway, without prior consultation
 and approval of the Commission. The Committee further recommends that the Commission of Railway Safety should
 submit half yearly reports to the Committee about the status of its recommendations indicating the discussions, if any,
 called by the Ministry of Railways on the issues of difference of opinion.         
(Recommendation at para 32)
18.       The Committee observes that a large number of new passenger trains are introduced every year to meet the
 demand of the traveling public. While it does fulfill the requirements of the public, it has to be examined as to whether
 such an action is in the interest of safety and convenience of the traveling public. The present system in the country is
 already overstressed and it is important to ensure that all infrastructure facilities cater to the safe running of additional
 trains with due safety margins. It is essential that such facilities are in position before adding any burden of additional
 trains. The introduction of additional trains involves the safety of the passengers. The Committee is not convinced with
 the reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways with regard to not seeking the concurrence of Commission of Railway
 Safety before introduction of a new passenger train. The Committee gives due weightage to the reply of the Ministry of
 Railways that before any new train is introduced, certification of available maintenance infrastructure at either end is
 given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and maintenance, after consulting all concerned
 agencies. Ministry of Railway have also pointed out that concurrence of every new train does not fall under the legal
 duties of Commission of Railway Safety, as enumerated in the Railway Act, 1989. The main task of the Commission is
 to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation/inspectional/audit and investigatory/advisory
 functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard to the soundness of rail
 construction and safety in train operation. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the sanction of Commission of
 Railway Safety must be necessary for Ministry of Railways before introducing any new passenger train. The
 Committee therefore, recommends that it should be made mandatory for Ministry of Railways to seek the concurrence
 of Commission of Railway Safety before introduction of any new passenger train, so as to ensure that the safety of the
 passengers is not compromised by amending the existing statutory provisions in this regard.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT

98thReport of Committeeon Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/98threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:11:25]
19.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation forwarded a copy of the recommendation made by the Committee to the Railway
 Board for their comments. The remarks of the Ministry of Railways and the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on
 the remarks of the Ministry of Railways are given below: -
20.       Remarks of Ministry of Railways: Introduction of new trains etc. is one of the executive functions of Ministry of
 Railways, which forms the routine business of rail transportation.  The Commission of Railway Safety has neither the
 wherewithal nor expertise to certify the various aspects to assess the adequacy of infrastructure and manpower etc.  It
 would not be desirable to burden the Commission with the newer an newer functions and it may perhaps be advisable
 for the Commission to devote its energies to discharge its duties envisaged in the Railways Act, 1989. 
21.       Views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the remarks of the Ministry of Railways:  Ministry of Railways’
 views have been noted.  However, it would be desirable that over loading of already saturated routes may be avoided
 since it may compromise the safety of passengers & Railway assets.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22.       The Committee notes the reply of Ministry of Railways and appreciates the fact that introduction of new trains
 etc. is one of the executive functions of Ministry of Railways. However, it appears that the recommendation of the
 Committee has not been understood properly. The Committee has no intention to authorise the Commission of Railway
 Safety to decide about the introduction of new passenger trains. The Committee has desired that before starting the
 actual operation of any passenger train, the safety aspects should be got approved from the Commission of Railway
 Safety. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendations that the existing statutory provisions should be
 amended to make it mandatory for the Ministry of Railways to seek the concurrence of Commission of Railway Safety
 before the introduction of any new passenger train. 
 
REVISION OF ‘RULES FOR OPENING, 1933’
(Recommendation at Para 37)
23.       The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Railways has, on the insistence of Commission of Railway
 Safety, decided to make necessary amendments in the present ‘Rules of 2000’ to include the ‘one month notice’ to the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety before any line is intended to be opened. The Committee recommends that the
 necessary amendment should be carried out at the earliest. The Committee further notes that the Ministry of Railways
 have decided to modify the extant rules so that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade should
 accompany the Commissioner of Railway Safety only in case the General Manager or the Principal Head of the
 Department are not able to accompany him due to unavoidable circumstances. However, the Committee would like to
 advise that an officer of the level of Senior Administrative Grade accompanying the Commissioner of Railway Safety
 on his inspection should remain an exception, as envisaged under the said provisions, than becoming the rule.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
24.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation forwarded a copy of the recommendation made by the Committee to the Railway
 Board for their comments. The remarks of the Ministry of Railways and the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on
 the remarks of the Ministry of Railways are given below: -
25.Remarks of Ministry of Railways: Necessary amendment has been carried out to the Railways (Opening for public
 carriage of passengers) Rules, 2000 to incorporate all the revisions as suggested by the Commission of Railway Safety.
26.Views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the remarks of the Ministry of Railways:  Since the recommendation has
 been accepted and implemented, no comments.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27.       The Committee notes the reply.
PUBLICATION OF REPORTS ON RAILWAY ACCIDENTS
(Recommendation at Para 52)
28.       The Committee is constrained to note that the inquiry reports of the Commission of Railway Safety on accidents
 are either not published or published too late and the people at large do not come to know of the reasons for
 concurrence of a particular accident. The Committee is of the view that the public needs to know the reasons for the
 Railway Accidents and it will serve the larger interest of the public if the accident reports are published at the earliest.
 The Committee also notes the impediments faced by the Commission of Railway Safety in undertaking the enquiries.
 The Committee feels that it is essential to provide legal protection to Commission of Railway Safety. The Committee is
 in agreement with the recommendations made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998, quoted at para 43 above.
 The Committee recommends that these recommendations should be accepted and the relevant acts and rules should be
 amended at the earliest. The Committee also recommends that when the Commission of Railway Safety proposes to
 take up an inquiry, inquiries initiated by police or magistrate should be stopped and the civil and police authorities

98thReport of Committeeon Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/98threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:11:25]
 should co-operate in the Commission’s inquiry. The Committee feels that the implementations of the steps suggested
 by the Committee will enable the Commissioners of Railway Safety in undertaking their inquiries without any
 hindrances. Thereby, the inquiry reports of the Commissioners on accidents could also be published as soon as the
 inquiry is over and the public at large would not be deprived of their vital right to information.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
29.       The recommendation made by the RSRC-98 about publication of Accident Inquiry Report and provision of legal
 immunity to the Commissioner of Railway Safety have been accepted. The Ministry has decided that the Report of the
 Commissioner can be made public once necessary provisions have been inserted in the Indian Railway Act 1989 to
 provide legal immunity. Amendment of the Act would need to be done by the Ministry of Railways.
30.       Meanwhile the Ministry has taken following decisions on the publication of Accident Inquiry Reports of the
 Commissioner of Railway Safety as an interim measure to restore public faith in the organization and to bring
 transparency in the system -
Ø
      To make all preliminary Reports of the Railway accidents inquired by the Commissioners public.
Ø      The inquiry reports of the accidents in which Railway Board’s comments have been received are being compiled
 in abstract form and published in six monthly periodicals starting from 1st January, 2004.
31.       The Committee’s observation about stopping the inquiry initiated by police and magistrate when the CRS
 decides to take up an inquiry will require necessary amendment in Railways Act, Indian Penal Code and other
 associated Acts/Codes/Rules. This will be examined further on receipt of comments of Railway Board.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
32.       The Committee notes the reply and recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should pursue the matter
 regarding the incorporation of suitable amendments in the Indian Railway Act, 1989 with Ministry of Railways to
 facilitate smooth and expeditious progress of inquiry proceedings and the immediate publication of inquiry reports of
 the Commission of Railway Safety on railway accidents. 
 
UPGRADATION OF STATUS OF OFFICERS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
(Recommendation at Para 60)
 
33.       The Committee is constrained to note that vacancies continue to exist in the Commission of Railway Safety for
 fairly long periods because of non-availability of eligible officers from the Ministry of Railways. The Committee
 recommends that any vacancy arising in the Commission of Railway Safety should be filled up at the earliest so that the
 functioning of the Commission does not suffer. The Committee is also constrained to note that the recommendations
 made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 are yet to be implemented by the Government. The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety, being the Principal Technical Advisor to the Government of India on matters
 concerning rail safety, is the highest technical official in the Ministry of Civil Aviation for dealing with railway safety.
 The Committee is of the view that upgradation of the post of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety to the level of
 Secretary to the Government of India is absolutely essential so that he can effectively and forcefully interact with the
 nine Secretary level officers of Railway Board. Lack of such a status to the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 works as a serious deterrent to him in discharging his duties effectively in a hierarchy conscious bureaucracy. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the status of Chief commissioner of Railway Safety should be equal to that of
 the Chairman of Railway Board in rank and pay. Likewise the status of Commissioner of Railway Safety should be
 equal to that of General Manager of a Zonal Railway in rank as well as pay. The posts of Deputy Commissioners of
 Railway Safety should be manned by Senior Administration Grade Officers. The Commissioners of Railway Safety
 should also be provided with the assistance of Deputy Commissioners. The Committee further recommends that, as
 recommended by the Fifth Central Pay Commission, the tenure of the Chief Commissioner should be five years, taking
 him beyond normal retirement age and upto 62 years. The Committee is of the firm view that these measures would
 bring to an end the current scenario of shortage of volunteers opting to join the Commission of Railway Safety. Also
 these measures will significantly enhance the status of the Commission, make it more dynamic and enable it to
 discharge its functions more effectively and its views heard and acted upon, with due importance by Railway
 Administration.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
34.       The proposals to upgrade the scale of pay of CCRS and CRS to that of Secretary to the Government of India &
 GM of Railways as also to provide a Dy. CRS with each CRS are under examination in the Ministry.

35.       Separately the Ministry is also examining a proposal to bring new Railway Safety Act with provision for a 3
 member Commission for Railway Safety on the lines of Election Commission of India. The concerns of the Committee
 would be taken care of to a large extent once the proposal in finalized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
36.       The Committee notes the reply and hopes that its observations/recommendations would be given due
 consideration before finalizing the proposals under examination in the Ministry so that the Commission of Railway
 Safety is accorded the desirable status and made a dynamic organization that commands the respect of the railway
 authorities and the public.
EXPOSURE TO TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCEMENTS
(Recommendation at Para 63)
37.       The Committee feels that there is a genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed
 to the latest technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad. Otherwise there is a real
 danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the Commission will get obsolete. The Committee recommends
 that the officers of the Commission should be exposed to latest technologies through trainings in the country and
 abroad, so that they are in a position to perform their role effectively. The officers of the Commission should also be
 given full facilities to become members of professional institutions, at par with the facilities extended by the Railway
 Administration to Railway Officers. This will help in keeping the officers of the Commission updated in their technical
 knowledge. However, for this purpose, the Commission should not depend upon the financial assistance of the Ministry
 of Railways. The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the budget of the Commission of
 Railway Safety should be suitably increased so that these requirements could be taken care of by the Commission itself.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
38.       A proposal to give facilities to the officers of the Commission to become members of professional institutions at
 par with the facilities extended by the Railway administration to Railway officers, is being examined. However the
 Ministry of Railways is being requested that CRS/Dy.CRS be given the exposure to latest technologies being developed
 in India & abroad. Commission of Railway Safety may also take initiative in this regard.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
39.       The Committee notes the assurance given by the Ministry and recommends that the Commission of Railway
 Safety may be directed to identify suitable training courses for its officers and send the proposal to the Ministry.
 
SUPPLY OF RAILWAY CIRCULARS ETC. TO COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
(Recommendation at Para 67)
40.       The Committee is of the view that unless the Commission of Railway Safety is kept aware of the latest
 instructions with respect to railway safety issued by the Railway Board or Zonal Railways, it cannot discharge its duties
 effectively. Ministry of Railways have admitted that copies of all important policy orders are endorsed to the Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways should ensure that
 Commission of Railway Safety is on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board and Zonal Railways for all policy
 Circulars having bearing on safety and all Circulars/Orders affecting safety. The Committee further recommends that
 the Commission of Railway Safety should be supplied with the proceeding of the Technical Committees of Railway
 Board so that the Commission remains informed of the safety problems encountered in the working of the railways and
 the measures taken to solve these problems.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
41.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation forwarded a copy of the recommendation made by the Committee to the Railway
 Board for their comments. The remarks of the Ministry of Railways and the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on
 the remarks of the Ministry of Railways are given below: -
42.       Remarks of Ministry of Railways: All policy Circulars, instructions, regulations etc. issued from Railway Board
 pertaining to Railway Safety are endorsed to the Commission of Railway Safety.
43.       Views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the remarks of the Ministry of Railways:  The proceedings of all the
 technical Committee of Railway Board having bearing on safety are not being sent.  Such proceeding, if made
 available, will give insight to the Commission, the basis of making a decision.  Railway Board will be pursued in the
 matter.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

 recommendation that the Commission of Railway Safety should be supplied with the proceeding of the Technical
 Committees of Railway Board so that the Commission remains informed of the safety problems encountered in the
 working of the railways and the measures taken to solve these problems.
LACK OF OFFICE INFRASTRUCTURE
(Recommendation at Para 69)
45.       The Committee notes with concern the constraints faced by the officers of the Commission of Railway Safety in
 performing their duties due to lack of budgetary allocations and proper infrastructure and office machinery. The
 Committee feels that the Commission of Railway Safety need adequate budgetary support from the Government so that
 it does not have to look upon the Ministry of Railways for being able to effectively discharge its duties. The Committee
 recommends that the budget allocation of Commission of Railway Safety should be substantially increased so that the
 Commission could take care of its essential requirements such as funds for foreign training, air travel within India,
 nominations to various training courses, membership to professional institution etc.        
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
46.       Any request for enhancement of the budget of Commission of Railway Safety would be forwarded to the
 Ministry of Finance for favorable consideration by them.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
47.       The Committee is unhappy about the indifferent attitude of the Ministry, as can be made out from the reply. It
 shows that the Ministry is unaware of the lack of budgetary allocations and proper infrastructure and office machinery
 required for the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety. The Committee recommends that the Ministry
 should take initiative for identifying and processing the financial requirements of the Commission and pursue it with
 the Ministry of Finance.   
ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRIMA-FACIE CAUSE OF ACCIDENTS BY RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION
(Recommendation at Para 71)
 
48.       The Committee is of the opinion that the unwritten convention that no one would give the cause of an accident,
 when an enquiry is pending, needs to be followed by the Railway Administration. The Committee recommends that the
 Railway administration should refrain from speculating and giving the prima-facie cause of an accident, which is
 required to be statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of Railway Safety. This will ensure that the credibility of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is maintained and the Commissioners are not suspected of prejudice or bias in
 conducting their enquiries.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
49.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation forwarded a copy of the recommendation made by the Committee to the Railway
 Board for their comments. The remarks of the Ministry of Railways and the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on
 the remarks of the Ministry of Railways are given below: -
 
50.       Remarks of Ministry of Railways:  In view of large scale public and media attention to the serious train accidents
 it is practically impossible not to announce prima facie cause based on the factual position.  This is however, is not
 speculative and it based on the preliminary facts and investigations carried out b the railway officers.  Announcement
 of prima facie cause has been in vogue from the time immemorial and does not interfere in the statutory inquiry in any
 way, which is later conducted by the Commission of Railway Safety.
 
51.       Views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the remarks of the Ministry of Railways:  The Ministry of Railways
 views have been noted.  However, it would be prudent to avoid making announcements regarding prima-facie cause of
 accidents.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
52.       The Committee notes the reply given by the Ministry of Railways and is of the opinion that a practice cannot
 earn legitimacy for the reason of it being inexistence for a long time.  The Railway authorities, if required, may clarify

 Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Railway administration should refrain from speculating
 and giving the prima-facie cause of an accident, which is required to be statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of
 Railway Safety.
 
CONCLUSION
(Recommendation at Para 72)
 
53.       The Committee is of the opinion that the Commission of Railway Safety is an important organization of the
 Government and, in the prevailing circumstances, the Commission’s hands need strengthening in all possible ways. The
 Committee recommends that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation incorporating the suggestion
 made by the Committee in this Report so that the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety could improve in
 the interest of the public travelling by Indian Railways.

 general impression that it is influenced by the Ministry of Railways. The Ministry has on the one hand claimed that the
 present arrangement of the Commission of Railway Safety being placed under the Ministry of Civil Aviation has been
 working satisfactorily since May, 1967 but on the other it has been stated that the present set up does not provide
 enough avenues to middle level officers for further advancement in the Commission, thereby railway officers would be
 unwilling to join the Commission on absorption basis. The Committee finds these submissions contradictory. The

 / Union Public Service Commission is under consideration. The Committee recommends that the said proposal should
 be expedited within a fixed timeframe and it should also include the aspect of comprehensive cadre review so that the
 impartiality and independence of the Commission is ensured.  (Para 12)

INTRODUCTION
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninety-ninth Report
 of the Committee on the Admiralty Bill 2005*.
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 11 th May 2005.  In pursuance of rules relating to the
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the
 Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, referred** the Bill to the Committee on 27th May 2005 for examination and report within
 three months. On the requests being made by the Chairman of the Committee, Hon’ble Chairman had granted extension
 of time till the 27th November, 2005, and then upto the 15th December, 2005, 28th February, 2006 and  28th April, 2006
 respectively for the presentation of the report of the Committee on the aforesaid Bill.
3.          The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Shipping and
 Ministry of Law and Justice at its meetings held on the      8th July 2005 and 28th September 2005 respectively.
4.         In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee invited the views of individuals, organisations and
 institutions on the subject through advertisement in all major national dallies and vernacular newspapers all over the
 country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda on the subject
 for consideration of the Committee.  The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of the Indian National
 Shipowners Associations, Foreign Owners Representative & Shipmanagers Association, Port, Dock and Waterfront
 Workers' Federation of India, All India Port and Dock Workers’ Federation, Indian National Port and Dock Workers’
 Federation, Iron Steel Scrap and Shipbreakers Association of India,  Company of Master Mariners of India and the
 National Union of Seafarers of India on the provisions of the Bill at its meetings held on the 18
th July, 19th July, 31 st
 August and 9th September 2005 respectively.
5.        The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill during its meeting held on the 17 th March
 2006.  The Committee also considered the draft Report on the subject and adopted the same with minor modifications
 on 17
th March 2006 itself.
6.          The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Shipping
 and Ministry of Law and Justice for the assistance provided during deliberations on the provisions of the Bill. The
 Committee also acknowledges the contribution of Shri Zarir P. Bharucha, Advocate, Supreme Court of India and the
 representatives of employees Unions/Federations/Associations of major ports, who submitted their valuable suggestions
 on the provisions of the Bill.

RE P O R T
 
The Admiralty Bill, 2005 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 11 th May, 2005.  The Bill seeks to update
 India's Admiralty Laws which would be responsive to the needs of the Industry and will ensure that the maritime
 disputes are disposed of expeditiously and effectively. The long title of the Bill highlights the purpose of the Bill as to

 Offences (Colonial) Act, 1849,  the Admiralty Jurisdiction (India) Act, 1860, the Admiralty Court Act 1861, the
 Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act, 1891 and  Patent relating to

Statement of Objects & Reasons:-
2.         The salient features given in the Statement of objects and reasons appended to the Admiralty Bill (Annexure)
 are as follows:-
      i.        The Admiralty laws in India are more than a century old and maritime industry has been highlighting the need to
 update India's admiralty laws to be responsive to the needs of the industry.
     ii.        To consolidate and amend the law relating to Admiralty jurisdiction of Courts, legal proceedings in connection
 with ships, their arrest, detention and sale and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
   iii.        To enlarge the scope of the legislation to cover claims pertaining to pollution damages, loss of life, personal
 injury, towage of ships, pilotage of ships, port dues, disbursement made by the ship owners and agents of ships.
   iv.        To make certain provision for vesting of civil jurisdiction in respect of various types of claims pertaining to
 shipping industry in High Courts, power of Supreme Court to transfer any proceedings from one High Court to
 another, power of the High Court to confer Admiralty jurisdiction in consultation with the Chief Justice of India
 on any Principal Civil Court of the State.
    v.        To spell out Admiralty jurisdiction and mode of exercising it, conditions in respect of claims in an action in rem,
 jurisdiction in personam, restrictions on entertainment of actions in cases pertaining to action in personam in
 collision of ships.
   vi.        To incorporate certain provision for vesting of rights on sale of ships, distribution of sale proceeds, order of
 priority of claim, maritime lien, procedure in respect of foreign ships and protection of owner, demise charterer,
 manager or operator of ships arrested.
 vii.        To apply Code of Civil Procedure, assistance of assessors, reference to arbitration and appeal.
viii.        To confer upon the Central Government the power to make rules besides provision for repeal of the existing laws
 on the subject as recommended by the Law Commission.
